CHAPTER I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1.  The Committee while extending its appreciation to the Election Commission of 
India for their diligent efforts in conducting free and fair elections in the country and 
recommends that citizens should have greater transparency when it comes to the 
Common Electoral Roll and the integration of Aadhaar with EPIC. However, it is 
important to note that linking Aadhaar with Voter ID is voluntary and not obligatory. 
(Para 1.48)   
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it may be stated that the said 
recommendation pertains to the ECI and they have submitted the comments as 
under:-  
1.3 Comments received from the ECI: “The Commission vide its letter no. 
23/inst/2022-ES dated 04.07.2022 has issued instructions to the CEOs of all the states 
and UTs for starting a programme to collect the Aadhar Number of the existing 
electors. A new Form 6B has been devised for electors who have already been 
enrolled in the electoral roll for providing their Aadhar details voluntarily. Further, 
the process of linking of Aadhaar with voter id has not been started yet. Further, the 
Commission is also considering amendments and modifications to the relevant 
provisions related to linking of Aadhar with Voter ID and enrolment Forms in view 
of Hon'ble Supreme Court's direction in the matter. It has been emphasised that the 
linking of Aadhaar with voter ID should be voluntary and not obligatory.” 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.4.  During discussions, some members of the Committee raised doubts about the 
linking of Aadhaar with EPIC of non-citizens, which led the Committee to suggest 
that the ECI should establish a legal provision or an alternative mechanism to ensure 
that non-citizens with Aadhaar are not included in the voter list. Additionally, citizens 
who have not yet linked their Aadhaar should be assured that they can still exercise 
their legal right to vote. The Committee emphasized the importance of these 
clarifications in addressing concerns related to the implementation of a Common 
Electoral Roll (Para 1.49) 

9 
 
Action Taken 
1.5 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it may be stated that the said 
recommendation pertains to the ECI and they have submitted the comments as under:-  
1.6 Comments received from the ECI: “As per Section 16 of RP Act, 1950 a non-
citizen is disqualified for registration in an electoral roll. Therefore, a non-citizen is 
not allowed to enroll even if he possesses Aadhaar card. Aadhar is not a citizenship 
document. Further, under Section 31 of the RP Act, 1950 making false declaration in 
connection with the preparation, revision or correction of an electoral roll or the 
inclusion or exclusion of any entry in or from an electoral roll is a punishable offence 
with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine or both. 
Hence, there is already legal provision available in the present election law to prevent 
a non-citizen from enrolment. 
1.7 For registration as an elector in an Assembly or Parliamentary Constituency, 
person must not be less than 18 years (on the qualifying date prescribed by law) and 
citizen of India having ordinarily resident in the constituency concerned. 
1.8 Further, vide Commission's letter dated 04.07.2022; it has been made amply 
clear that submission of Aadhaar by electors is voluntary and their names cannot be 
struck off from the electoral database merely because of their inability to furnish 
Aadhaar.” 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
1.9  The Committee recommends that the Legislative Department and the Election 
Commission collaborate to examine the effects of the delimitation process, especially 
in challenging terrains. The Election Commission lacks the authority to direct State 
Election Commissions or appraise the performance of State Election Commissioners. 
The Committee draws the attention of ECI to the fact that treating all regions in India 
as identical can pose a significant risk. It is therefore imperative to recognize this 
reality and take appropriate measures to address it. (Para 1.55) 
Action Taken  
1.10 Comments received from the ECI: “The recommendations of the Committee 
have been noted for future reference.” 
1.11 Comments of this Department: The recommendations of the Committee have 
been noted for future reference. 
 

10 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.12 The Committee has taken note of the potential benefits that could be derived 
from the creation of a Common Electoral Roll through the collaborative participation 
of officials who serve in both the Election Commission of India and State Election 
Commissions. However, it stresses the importance of proper constitutional and 
statutory authorization before the Election Commission takes charge of creating or 
managing electoral rolls for State Election Commissions. The Committee suggests 
that States may continue to utilize the electoral roll of the Election Commission until 
necessary legal changes have been made. Furthermore, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Election Commission of India and the Legislative Department 
collaborate to preserve the rights of both State Election Commissions and State 
Governments when preparing the Common Electoral Roll. (Para 1.56) 
Action Taken  
1.13 Comments received from the ECI: “In this connection, it is informed that ECI 
facilitates State Election Commissions by sharing its electoral roll data with them 
upon their request in the manner and form as requested, on which SECs carry out 
their amendments or marking of ward boundaries. 
1.14 So far, Election Commission of India has shared its Electoral roll data with 32 
State Election Commissions.” 
1.15 Comments of this Department: It is stated that the recommendations of the 
Committee have been noted by this Department. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.16.  The Committee suggests that the Election Commission and Legislative 
Department collaborate to encourage States to utilize the Election Commission's 
electoral roll when creating their own until there is a change in constitutional and 
statutory provisions. The Committee strongly emphasizes the significance of 
preserving the rights of State Election Commissions and State while taking action. 
(Para 1.57) 
  

11 
 
Action Taken  
1.17 Comments received from the ECI: “The ECI facilitates State Election 
Commissions by sharing its electoral roll data with them upon their request in the 
manner and form as requested, on which SECs carry out their amendments of 
marking of ward boundaries. So far, Election Commission of India has shared its 
Electoral roll data with 32 State Election Commissions.” 
1.18 Comments of this Department: It is stated that the recommendations of the 
Committee have been noted by this Department. Further, it is stated that the reply to 
paragraph 4 may be again referred to.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.19  The Committee observes that it is important to involve stakeholders in the 
process of creating fair regulations for defining reasonable declarations in election 
affidavits. This is crucial to protect innocent individuals and distinguish fraudulent 
declarations from unintentional mistakes. To ensure fair and effective elections, it is 
necessary to address the challenges faced by political parties and candidates. (Para 
2.30) 
Action Taken  
1.20 Comments received from the ECI: “Political parties may be asked to provide 
their views in the matter. Ministry of Law & Justice may please consider.” 
1.21 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that this Department 
has taken note of the recommendation of the Committee to address the challenges 
faced by the political parties and candidates during filing of the election affidavits. It 
is further stated that the recommendations of the Committee would be referred in 
future as and when electoral reforms are carried out on the issue. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.22  The Committee strongly recommends that the RP Act of 1951 needs to have a 
clear definition of what constitute a false declaration/affidavit which is presently 
mentioned under Section 123(4) that covers corrupt practices, and concealment of 
information specified under Section 125A which specifies penalties for filing false 
affidavits respectively, so as to establish fair practices in election process. (Para 2.31) 
  

12 
 
Action Taken 
1.23 Comments received from the ECI: “Noted in the Commission. 
Further, the Commission vide letter no. 3/1/2011/5DR dated 3rd February, 2011 
(Annexure-B) (Reiterated in April, 2012) had already proposed an amendment to Sec 
125 A of 1951 Act, providing for punishment of 2 years imprisonment for filing of 
false affidavits by the candidates (Affidavit in Form 26) and to include this in sub-
section (1) of section 8 so that conviction will automatically lead to disqualification.” 
1.24 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that this Department 
has noted the recommendation of the Committee and whenever the proposals for 
electoral reforms are taken up by the Government the ECI’s proposal for amending 
the provision regarding false declaration shall also be considered. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.25  The Committee also recommends that the penalties associated with these 
actions should be based on their severity of the act committed and be included as a 
separate provision in addition to or in place of the existing Section 125A that deals 
with penalties for false declarations. (Para 2.32) 
Action Taken 
1.26 Comments received from the ECI: “For providing different penalties, based on 
severity of the act committed, the information provided in the affidavit is required to 
be categorized. Ministry of Law & Justice may take a view.” 
1.27 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that this Department 
has taken note of the recommendation of the Committee. It is further stated that the 
recommendations of the Committee would be referred in future as and when electoral 
reforms are carried out on the above mentioned issue. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.28  The Committee also recommends that if a candidate is found to have provided 
false Information, under the updated/new provision proposed by the Committee, they 
should be deemed ineligible for any benefits resulting from such election. This 
measure is aimed at ensuring a level playing field for all candidates and upholding 
the integrity of the election process. (Para 2.34) 
  

13 
 
Action Taken 
1.29 Comments received from the ECI: “The Commission has already proposed to 
include filing of false declaration/ affidavit in connection with election in sub-section 
(1) of section 8 so that conviction will automatically lead to disqualification.” 
1.30 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that this Department 
has taken note of the recommendation of the Committee. It is further stated that the 
recommendations of the Committee would be referred in future as and when electoral 
reforms are carried out on the above mentioned issue. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
1.31  The Committee also recommends the removal of the phrase “with the intent to 
be elected in an election” from the section 125A as it creates legal ambiguity in 
finalizing the penalty. (Para 2.38)  
Action Taken 
1.32 Comments received from the ECI:  “Noted in the Commission.” 
1.33 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that this Department 
has taken note of the recommendation of the Committee. It is further stated that the 
recommendations of the Committee would be referred in future as and when electoral 
reforms are carried out on the above mentioned issue. 
  

14 
 
CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF 
THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2.1.  Due to the significant delays in addressing electrol reforms and the lack of 
progress made since the Election Commission of India proposed the Common 
Electoral Roll to the Prime Minister in 1999 and 2004, resulting in a delay of about 
20-23 years, the Committee recommends that the ECI develop a comprehensive plan 
that considers all the factors involved in implementing a Common Electoral Roll 
before making any changes to the current regulations. (Para 1.50) 
Action Taken 
2.2 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it may be stated that the said 
recommendation pertains to the ECI and they have submitted the comments as 
under:-  
2.3 Comments received from the ECI: “In this regard, it is submitted that

Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.1.  For elections to be truly free and fair, it is crucial to ensure that accurate 
information is provided to voters. The Supreme Court recognizes this importance and 
this Committee emphasizes the need to define what is considered a False 
Declaration/affidavit and when penalties, criminal action, or disqualification are 
warranted. It's important to note that minor factual errors should not be treated as 
significant enough to require penalization. (Para 2.28) 
Action Taken 
3.2 Comments received from the ECI: “Sec 125A of the Representation of the 
People Act, 1951 defines false declaration in connection with an election. Section 
125A provides that: 
"A candidate who himself or through his proposer, with intent to be elected in an 
election:- 
(1) fails to furnish information relating to sub-section (1) of section 33A; or 
(ii) gives false information which he knows or has reason to believe to be false; or 
(iii) conceals any information, in his nomination paper delivered under sub-section 
(1) of section 33 or in his affidavit which is required to be delivered under sub-
section (2) of section 33A, as the case may be, shall, notwithstanding anything 
contained in any other law for the time be in force, be punishable with imprisonment 
for a term which may extend to six months or with fine, or with both. 
3.3 It is for the Ministry of Law & Justice to define as to what constitute false 
information.” 
  

25 
 
Further recommendation/observation: 
3.4 The Committee notes that while the existing legal provision under Section 
125A does address the issue of false declarations, the lack of clarity and 
standardisation in interpreting “false information” continues to create 
ambiguity in enforcement. The ECI’s response, though legally valid, is 
procedurally insufficient, as it does not reflect a proactive approach in aiding 
legislative clarity or suggesting improvements in the operational framework.  
ECI, being the nodal authority on election administration, is best positioned to 
recommend technical and procedural refinements, offer a detailed proposal and 
assist the Ministry to frame clear provision, in this regard. 
Recommendation/Observation 
 
3.5  The Committee proposes that candidates who provide false information in their 
affidavits should be disqualified or declared ineligible, depending upon the severity 
of the action committed, regardless of whether they win the election.  The Committee 
believes this is essential to uphold the integrity of the democratic processes in 
accordance with the Constitutional mandate. The Committee recommends that the 
government sets up a verification process for affidavits and promptly informs the 
Election Commission of any false data to ensure adherence to regulations. (Para 2.29)

26

been made in the Para 3.20, 3.21 and 3.22 of the report and action on the Para 3.23 of 
the report pertain to Government of India.” 
3.27 Comments of this Department: In this regard, it is stated that the 
recommendations of the Committee at Paragraphs 3.20, 3.21 and 3.22 of the report 
are general observations of the committee and hence, require no action and thus, do 

30 
 
not warrant a specific reply by this Department. It is further, stated with respect to 
recommendation at paragraph 3.23 of the Committee Report it is stated that this 
Department concurs with the view of Election Commission on the above mentioned 
issue which has been stated in the following in Paragraph 3.11 at page 47 of the 
report and reads as under:- 
3.28 “According to the Election Commission of India, unless compelling reasons 
exist to alter a provision of the Constitution, it should remain unchanged. The 
Commission believes that this principle falls under the age requirement for eligibility 
to join Lok Sabha, Rajya Sabha, Legislative Assemblies, and Legislative Councils. 
The Commission has already considered the issue of aligning the minimum age for 
voting and contesting elections to Parliament, State Legislature, and local bodies and 
has found that it is unrealistic to expect 18-year-olds to possess the necessary 
experience and maturity for these responsibilities. Therefore, the minimum age for 
voting and contesting elections is appropriate. The Commission does not favour 
reducing the age requirement for membership of Parliament and State Legislatures 
and still maintains this view.”  
 
[Emphasis Supplied]  
 
3.29 Hence, in view of the Department this recommendation of the Committee does 
not appear to be feasible. 
Further recommendation/observation: 
3.30 The Committee recommends that the Department reconsider the proposal 
in view of evolving democratic trends and international practices that 
increasingly encourage youth participation in governance. For this, a 
comprehensive consultation process should be initiated, involving youth 
organizations, constitutional experts, and civil society stakeholders. 
Additionally, the feasibility of a phased or limited reduction in the minimum 
age, such as lowering it to 21 years, may be explored through a structured 
impact study to assess potential implications and benefits.

the way in which competitive exams are conducted. (Para 2.47)

with various States/ Organization including consultation with stakeholders. NRA

Chairman, SSC is an esteemed Member of General Body of NRA. The experiences 
and expertise of SSC in holding recruitment examinations have been shared to 
enable NRA to finalize the modalities involved in the process of conducting the 
exams. 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.2    The Committee also recommends that NR A should consult Railway 
Recruitment Board as well regarding the recruitment proposal being prepared, so 
that NRA can finish the task within the given timeline and without any criticism.

CHAPTER II 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE 
COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF 
THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.0       The Committee observes that UPSC and SSC conduct various examinations 
each year and allocate recommended candidates to different posts. For instance, 
through the Civil Services examination, UPSC selects about 1000 candidates every 
year and these candidates are posted across 19 different services.  With reference to 
this the Committee notes that the same process and yardstick is being applied t o 
select candidates who would be manning the top administrative posts in various 
services. It may happen sometime that the aptitude and interest of the candidate 
selected may not be suitable for that particular post.(Para 2.4) 
Action Taken 
2.1   Union Public Service Commission  conducts the Civil Services Examination 
strictly in accordance with the provisions contained in the Rules of the Examination 
and recommends the candidates on the basis of the merit. The candidates selected 
by UPSC through the Civil Services Examination are allocated services as per their 
rank and preference. The concerned Cadre Controlling Authorities (CCAs) 
provides requisite training to the candidates on/before their joining the post which 
is devised by the CCAs taking in account the nature of duties assigned to the post to 
develop the required skill needed to do the work allocated to the post in their 
Department. 
2.2 Recruitment examinations, conducted by Staff Selection Commission caters to 
posts which have similarity in pay level, educational qualification, age and other 
aspects of recruitment rules. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.3 The Committee observes and appreciates that with changing times, the 
Government has brought in several significant changes in the training methodology. 
However, the efficiency, energy and intensity of the officers still needs to improve 
and the officers need to be further trained for working in adverse situations, 
particularly to tackle law and order problems effectively. (Para 2.11)             

18 
 
Action Taken 
2.4 The National Programme for Civil Services Capacity Building (NPCSCB)/ 
Mission Karmayogi with the vision of citizen centric and future ready civil service is 
working towards competency driven capacity building for enabling the civil servants 
to prov ide effective public service delivery. Capacity Building Commission (CBC) 
will create along with the relevant CTIs, case studies and best practices and refresher 
courses on this and associated subjects. These will be on IGOT so that anyone can 
access these courses as and when they need. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.5 The Committee feels that a Civil Servant is an interface between the 
government and common public and works at the grassroot  level which requires 
considerable human touch and sensitive approach towards the people. He/ she works 
among the poor people most of the times and not the elite. If there is lack of 
sensitivity one cannot be a good administrator. So, Committee wishes to e mphasize 
that the civil servant has to be given training in such a way that he develops a more 
humane and empathetic approach towards any issue. The Committee also observed 
that the present day civil servant did not possess the same legal prowess as their 
predecessors. (Para 2.12)  
Action Taken 
 
2.6 Training Division, DoPT, has informed that the Capacity Building 
Commission (CBC)has initiated a series of citizen centric behavioural  improvement 
courses covering over 300,000 Railway Employees, U.T. Police Forces, Gramin Dak 
Sevak, Income Tax Officials. This could be incorporated as part of the foundation 
course at LBSNAA and other cen tral training institutes like NAIR, NADT, NACIN 
and could also be given to the civil servants at various points in their careers. CBC 
has the details of the courses. These also include courses for behavioral competency 
development that inter -alia contribute towards developing a human and empathetic  
approach towards issues encountered by the Civil Servants.   
Recommendation/Observation 
2.7 The Committee feels that there is a need to impart better training in the legal 
part as they are also quasi-judicial officers so that the officers when they take the final 
assignment, address the judicial problems more meticulously than what they are doing 
nowadays. (Para 2.14)            

19 
 
Action Taken 
2.8 LBSNAA is doing this as part of induction program. CBC will add refresher 
courses on IGOT for the legal part so that officers can refresh their knowledge as and 
when needed. Further CBC has partnered ministries/ department to create know your 
ministry online training which incorporates basics of the legal provisions 
administrated by department e.g. Department of Food and Public Distribution or 
Deportment of Consumer Affairs. 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.9 The Committee feels that rendering services to common people is the primary 
task of the Civil Servants and inclinati on to serve the society with human touch must 
be an essential quality amongst the Civil Servants. The Committee therefore, 
recommends that while examinations are conducted and the question paper is 
prepared, these factors also need to be taken into account  apart from the subject and 
intelligence. The Committee is of the view that these factors probably could help in 
moulding the prospective/selected candidate to work for betterment of the society.  
(Para 2.16)               
Action Taken 
2.10 Union Public Service Commission has informed that the topics prescribed 
in the General Studies Paper -IV (Ethics, Integrity and Aptitude) of the Civil 
Services (Main) Examination by and large address the mentioned issues. The detail 
of the syllabus of this Paper-IV is attached as Annexure II. 
2.11 The scheme and syllabus of mandated open competitive examinations 
conducted by Staff Selection Commision are based on the recommendations of the 
Expert Committee. 
2.12 Ministry of Home Affairs,  has accepted the recommendations of the 
Committee and issued appropriate directions in respect of recruitment made in 
Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs). 
INDIAN ARMY 
 
2.13  (a) Officer Entry. All candidates applying for officer entries are 
evaluated for 15 Officer Like Qualities (OLQs) through a three pronged 
psychological evaluation during the selection process in the Services Selection Board 
(SSB). Social Adjustment, Cooperation and Sense of Responsibility are three 

20 
 
important OLQs for which each candidate is tested and only those found suitable are 
selected. 
 
(b) Agniveers. The Indian Army is introducing psychometric tests as part 
of the recruitment process. Defence Institute of Psychological Research (DIPR) is 
formalizing the user module to include the aspect of teamwork and social adaptability 
with an aim to select candidates having inclination to seek and enjoy the company of 
other people, having a friendly disposition, receiving as well as extending 
cooperation willingly and likely for working as member of a team for achieving the 
goals. It includes cooperation, accommodating, team spirit, adaptability, empathy and 
emotional stability. 
INDIAN NAVY 
 
2.14 The requirement of rendering service to common people brought out in the 
concerned paragraph is in the context of an essential quality in the Civil Servants. 
Military Services, on the other hand, places even higher demands on individuals who 
need to be ready to make the ultimate sacrifice for  his/ her country. Recruitment in 
the Armed Forces intrinsically imbibes these ethos and the personnel joining are 
expected to possess them. Further, the implementation of projective techniques in the 
officer’s selection as well as the physical and mental stress of the sailor’s recruitment 
process, enable adequate assessment of candidates on these grounds.

2.27 1 (a) The Union Public Service Commission , a Constitutional Body, is 
mandated to carry out a wide range of functions under Article 320 of the 
Constitution of India. These functions, inter -alia, include (i) conduct of 
examinations for appointment to the services of the Union; (ii) direct recruitment 
by selection through Interviews; (iii) appointment of officers on promoti on/ 
deputation/ absorption; (iv) framing and amendment of Recruitment Rules for 
various services and posts under the Government; (v) disciplinary cases relating to 
different Civil Services & (vi) besides, advising the Government on any matter 
referred to t he Commission by the President of India. In the discharge of this 
constitutional mandate UPSC is solely governed by merit, duly reinforced by the 
principles of equity, justice and fair play. 
(b)       The defending cases pending before the various courts a cross the 
country where action(s) of the Commission has been challenged by the aggrieved 
parties pertain to the matters/ issues indicated in para 1(a) above. 
         (i) Examinations and Recruitment Tests: UPSC is entrusted with 
conducting structured exam inations and direct recruitments as per the rules of the 
examinations, recruitment rules/service rules notified by the Government of India 
in the nodal Ministries/ Departments concerned. These rules prescribe, inter -alia, 

23 
 
the eligibility conditions, scheme s and syllabus of the examinations, age, 
qualifications etc. Applications received are thoroughly scrutinized in the 
Commission, as per extant rules. The majority of the court cases relate to the 
eligibility conditions, rejection of applications/candidature. Mediation or arbitration 
with any petitioner is not feasible as this may require relaxation/amendment in the 
extant rules notified by the concerned Ministries/ Departments. Without relaxing/ 
amending these rules no relief can be granted to any petitione r in the above cases. 
Therefore, settlement in such Court Cases through mediation or arbitration is not 
feasible. 
        (ii)   Recruitment Rules/Service Rules:      UPSC is an advisory body 
and renders advice on proposals for framing/ amendment of Recrui tment Rules/ 
Service Rules brought before it by the Administrative Ministry/ Department after 
due concurrence/ approval of DoPT. The same is processed as per extant DoPT 
guidelines and advice of the Commission is issued accordingly. In cases where a 
petitioner has challenged the Recruitment Rules/ Service Rules of an 
Administrative Ministry/ Department, UPSC is mostly made a Proforma party and 
no action on part of UPSC generally lies in such cases. 
         (iii)  Disciplinary matters : With regard to cases relating to advice 
rendered by the Commission pertaining to disciplinary cases, it is the Disciplinary 
Authority (DA), who after considering the advice of UPSC and the representation 
of the Charged Officer (CO) thereon, imposes the penalty on the CO. It is  for the 
DA to accept or disagree with the recommendation/ advice of the Commission. 
Being aggrieved with the penalty imposed, the CO/ applicant approaches the CAT/ 
Court challenging penalty order. In most of the cases, Administrative Ministry is 
impleaded as main respondent, and UPSC is cited as proforma respondent. The 
directions/ decisions passed by the CAT/ Courts in such cases are mainly for 
Administrative Ministry to implement and the UPSC has no role in granting relief 
to the applicant/ petitioner. 
        (iv) Selection of SCS Officers to AIS : The proposals for 
promotions/ selections of State Civil Service (SCS)/ State Police Service (SPS)/ 
State Forest Service (SFS) to the Indian Administrative Service (IAS)/ Indian 
Police Service (IPS)/ Indian Forest Service (IFS) are received from the concer ned 
State Governments/ UTs. The promotions/ selections are done after following 
respective Promotion Regulations and the guidelines formulated by the 
Commission in consultation with other Ministry/ Departments of Government of 
India. 

24 
 
In case of Director Ge neral of Police (DGP), there have been separate 
guidelines, drawn in line with the Supreme Court directions/ orders, from time to 
time. 
        (v) Promotion/Deputation: Recommendations of the Commission are 
conveyed on the basis of DPCs/ SCM (PTs) in acco rdance with the guidelines and 
rules issued by the Govt. of India as amended from time to time. Aggrieved parties 
in such cases are the officials from the Center/ State Services challenging the 
outcome of DPCs/ SCM (PTs). Representatives of various stake holders viz. UPSC, 
DoPT and State Governments form part of DPCs/ SCM (PTs). It is worthwhile to 
mention here that after thorough scrutiny and consideration of all the relevant 
aspects a candidate is recommended fit or unfit by DPCs/ SCM (PTs). Mediation or 
arbitration with any petitioner is not feasible as this would require review of DPCs/

applicant in most of the cases is not feasible, hence the matter of framing a policy

shortly to enhance participation of women in ICG. Subsequently, the women officers 
and Eps (enrolled personnel) will be deputed onboard afloat units for which 
modification onboard commissioned af loat units (Class of ship) is under active 
consideration. Further, suitable women friendly SQR’s (Standard Qualitative 
Requirement) are being amended for ships under construction/ to be constructed at 
various shipyards. Measures for Gender Sensitization are also being undertaken. 
BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION  

51 
 
2.119 Working conditions of the Border Roads Organisation are unique compared to 
other Civil  organisation and most of the Units/Formations are located in far flung 
Areas in adverse weather and terrain conditions. Accordingly, the number of women 
Group ‘A’ officers is less in the Border Roads Organisation. At present 19 women 
GREF officers  are ser ving in the Border Roads Organisation. Various initiatives 
regarding women empowerment have been started in the Organisation. Various 
factors are analysed while issuing posting of women officers, and in most of the cases 
it is endeavour of the department t o give women officers softer posting comparative 
to the male counterparts. However, due to paucity of units/formations located in 
softer areas, women officers are also being posted to High Altitude and Hard Areas as

2.120 As per posting policy of the organisation, the lady employees on completion of 
their tenure are asked to furnish five choice stations for their posting, accordingly, the 
lady employees are being posted. Moreover, the lady employees are also posted on

employees. At present 451 female subordinate employees  are serving with the 
department.  
Recommendation/Observation 
 2.121 The Committee also recommends that some sort of reservation may also be 
given to Transgenders. Steps may be taken to recruit transgenders as well so that 
they can be integrated well with mainstream society in near future.  (Para 2.92) 
Action Taken

reservation for Transgender Persons is Sub Judice in the Supreme Court of India. 
Recommendation/Observation  
2.123 The Committee recommends that with respect to border districts, it is 
paramount to recruit maximum youngsters from these areas. Special recruitment 
drives may be conducted for recruitment of local youngsters from states like 
Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, North Eastern states and Kashmir. It should be ensured 
that the 25 per cent of reservation for areas affected by militancy/LWE and 25% 
vacancies of border guarding forces allotted to border districts is fulfilled 
immediately so that the energy and talent of yout h of these areas are channelized 
and they do not deviate toward extremism and terrorism.  (Para 2.96) 

52 
 
Action Taken  
2.124 Ministry of Home Affairs  has stated that, as per policy, 25% vacancies in

for  Border districts falling in Area of Responsibility (AOR) of forces and   25% 
vacancies are earmarked for LWE/Militancy affected areas in the Constable(GD) 
Examination.  Provisions already exist for conducting special recruitment rallies in 
border districts and militancy/LWE affected areas after conclusion of recruitment 
process for Constable (GD) examination by SSC. Recently, the following special 
recruitment rallies have been conducted: 
i. In 2021, against 1356 vacancies, 1355 candidates were recruited 
from 22 districts of J&K and Ladakh. 
ii. In the year 2022, special recruitment rally was conducted to 
recruit 400 tribals youths as Constable (GD) in CRPF from three 
districts of Chhattisgarh namely Bajpur , Dantwada , Sukma. 
2.125 Further approval has already been accorded to conduct special rally/drive to 
fill up 620 unfilled vacancies of Constable(GD) Examination, 2022 in the Border

Recommendation/Observation 
2.126 The Committee recommends that regular studies should be undertaken to 
prevent any kind of stagnation at various levels of promotion. Cadre Review of 
each Para -Military Force must be conducted in every five years without fail. A

there is stagnation in promotion at any level or there is no further scope of

CHAPTER III 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF 
WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS 
GIVEN BY THE GOVERNMENT AND REITERATES ITS 
RECOMMENDATION 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.0 The Committee notes that it is quite evident from the table, the maximum 
number of officers recruited are from Technical and medical background. Above 70 
per cent of the recruits in the civil service by UPSC nowadays are from technical 
streams. Every year, hundreds of technocrats are thus being lost, who are likely to 
work in other specific areas which is also a requirement for the nation.   So, doctors 
and top technocrats are being lost who can perform as very good doctors and 
engineers.  The allurement to become civil servant is perhaps also adversely aff ecting 
other fields of working.   Hence, the Committee opines that it is high time to have a 
rethink about the whole process of recruitment for the Civil Service. (Para 2.7)          
Action Taken 
3.1 Union Public Service Commission has constituted Expert Committees in 
consultation with the Government from time to time in the past to assess the efficacy 
in selecting the most suitable candidates through the Civil Services Examination. 
Based on the recomm endations of such Committees, necessary changes have been 
carried out in scheme of Civil Services Examination accordingly. The last such 
Committee i.e. Baswan Committee, was constituted on 12 -08-2015 which submitted 
its report on 09 -08-2016. The Commission  conveyed its views on the 
recommendations of the Baswan Committee in March, 2017 to Department of 
Personnel and Training, for consideration. The Report of the Baswan Committee is 
under consideration in the DoPT. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.2 The Committee notes that the each recruitment test conducted by UPSC as of 
now, takes anywhere between six months to one year to complete. This long drawn 
process involves a lot of expenses for the competing candidates and also 
contributes to the erosion of human cap ital. In view of this, the Committee desires 

55 
 
to know whether UPSC is contemplating to make any change in the pattern of civil 
services examination to curtail the length of the examination cycle.      (Para 2.9)  
Action Taken 
3.3 It has been the constant endeavour of Union Public Service Commission  to 
compress the time -cycles of all its Examinations including the Civil Services 
Examination. The examination process involves several steps including 
Notification of Examination Rules a s well as reporting of vacancies by the 
Government. The Commission publishes the Calendar of Examinations well in 
advance, as per which these Examinations are conducted. 
3.4 As regards the Civil Services Examination, following are submitted: 
(a)       This Examination has following stages (i) Preliminary Examination 
(Objective type) for screening of candidates for the Civil Services (Main) 
Examination (ii) Civil Services (Main) Examination (Descriptive type) and (iii) 
Personality Test/Interview. A statement showing the time taken at different stages of 
the Examination during the period from 2017 –2021, i.e. from the stage of 
advertisement (Notification of the Examination) to declaration of final result is 
attached as Annexure I. 
 
(b)       As per the current  trend, number of applications for the Civil Services 
(Preliminary) Examination comes to over a million every year. The 2023 
Examination was held at 79 Centres (cities) across the country at 2,538 Venues to 
accommodate 10.27 lakh candidates. For ensuring s mooth conduct of this 
Examination, numerous activities are required to be completed by the Commission 
viz. (i) selection of Venues in each Centre; (ii) processing/ scrutiny of applications 
received in order to allow only eligible candidates; (iii) distribu tion of candidates 
(after availability of exact count on completion of application process) to these 
Venues; (iv) preparation and release of e -Admit Cards of the candidates; (v) 
preparation of Scannable Attendance Lists of candidates, printing and dispatch  of the 
same to the Venue Supervisors; (vi) packing/dispatch of OMR sheets/stationeries to 
the Venues; (vii) preparation/ despatch of sensitive material to the Centres; (viii) 
deployment of large number of examination functionaries at different levels to t hese 
centres and venues; (ix) release of funds to the Centres and Venues; (x) conduct of 
meetings with various stake holders like police, postal authorities, railway authorities, 
Centre Supervisors, Inspecting Officers etc.; (xi) issue of number of   letters from 
different levels to number of authorities etc. 

56 
 
(c)        All these processes are to be executed with extreme care following 
various checks &  counter-checks at different levels in coordination with the 
examination functionaries to rule out any possibility of any error/mistake at any 
stage. It would be seen from the attached statement that the time duration for such 
activities has been within the range of around 2.5 to 3 months. Hence, this much lead 
time is a bare minimum for successful conduct of Examination of this scale. It may, 
thus, be appreciated that there is hardly any scope for further compressing the time 
between the date of advertisem ent (notification) and date of holding the Civil 
Services (Preliminary) Examination owing to the reasons cited above. 
  
(d)       After taking due care and completing all the processes, presently result 
of the Preliminary Examination is declared within 12 days from the date of conduct 
of the Examination. Earlier, time taken to declare the result was somewhere between 
40-50 days. Again, for smooth conduct of the Main Examination, which is a 5 days 
affair having 9 descriptive type papers, the drills of arrang ement are almost the same 
as those of the Preliminary Examination except the level of scale involved. The 
average time gap between declaration of the result of the Preliminary Examination 
and conduct of the Main Examination is about 2 -3 months. At this sta ge, the 
Preliminary Examination Qualified Candidates are needed adequate time to prepare 
for the Main Examination because of the number of papers and their toughness level. 
Any attempt to reduce this gap may invite grievances from the candidates. Therefore , 
there is hardly any possibility to bring down this time gap of three months. 
 
(e)       The Civil Services (Main) Examination, being a 9 Papers -Examination 
of descriptive type, it takes more time for evaluation of answer scripts i.e. about more 
than two months as nearly 1.20 lakh scripts of different subjects are evaluated by 
different teams of experts. Therefore, at this stage also, there is little scope of 
reducing the time-line between the date of completion of the Main Examination and 
the declaration of its result. 
 
(f)        After declaration of result of the Main Examination, as per existing 
scheme, the successful candidates are required to fill up Detailed Application Form 
(DAF-II) for which, time is given to them. Once these  DAFs-II are received from 
them, the same are processed for generation of E -Summon Letter and scheduling of 
their Personality Tests. The Personality Tests are held at the UPSC, so the candidates 
are required to come to the UPSC for attending the same from their places of stay 
across the country. Therefore, a lead time is to be given to them for arranging their 
transport, necessary documents and stay in Delhi. As such, the Personality Tests 

57 
 
cannot be scheduled immediately after the declaration of result of t he Main 
Examination. Further, maximum 12 candidates are interviewed in a day by one 
Personality Test Board, which is the optimal number which cannot be increased in 
order to maintain the quality of the Personality Test process and awarding of marks to 
the candidates as per their skills and capabilities. Besides, these Personality Test 
Boards are chaired by the Hon’ble Members of the Commission. Hence, the number 
of such Boards depends on the availability of Hon’ble Members. Furthermore, the 
entire duration of the Personality Test process is dependent on this aspect as also on 
the number of candidates, which in turn depends on the number of vacancies to be 
filled up on the basis of the Examination. On completion of the Personality Tests, 
final result of the Civil Service Examination is declared within 4 days. As such, there 
is also hardly any scope of reducing the time -line for completion of Personality Test 
process. 
 
(g)       It may be seen that the time cycle for the Civil Services Examination 
has been opti mized to the extent possible despite increase in the number of 
candidates, Centres and Venues over the years after analysing the time taken in the 
pre-examination and post examination activities in detail. One of the most vital 
factors that go into the det ermination of the time schedule of an Examination is the 
need to maintain the utmost confidentiality and the integrity of the examination 
process. Various checks and balances have been integrated in the examination 
system, which have been gained through ye ars of experience to eliminate the risk to 
the confidentiality and integrity, so that the Examination is conducted in an utmost 
fair and transparent manner. 
3.5 Further, it may also be appreciated that the UPSC presently holds another 12 
Structured Examinations and, therefore, it takes due care to also keep the time cycle 
of these Examinations at the optimum level besides optimizing the time cycle of the 
Civil Services Examination. Further, the UPSC ensures that a judicious balance is 
maintained at all stag es of all its Examinations including the Civil Services 
Examination. 
3.6 Furthermore, this issue was also referred to the Baswan Committee. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.7      The Committee earnestly recommends a comprehensive re -examination 
of civil services recruitment framework. The objective is to strike a careful 
balance between drawing exceptional talent into public administration and 
retaining the country’s finest doctors, engineers, and technocrats in the fields 

58 
 
where their skills are irreplaceable. At present, the examination cycle stretches 
across almost an entire year. This not only delays the entry of competent officers 
into service but also compels highly skilled professionals to step away from their 
core vocations for prolonged periods. The nation quietly loses valuable expertise 
in medicine, engineering, and other vital sectors. Therefore, the Committee 
believes the recruitment process must be rationalised and streamlined. Its 
duration should be curtailed. Stages of as sessment must be harmonised to 
improve efficiency, without compromising the integrity or quality of selection. 
Moreover, new and flexible pathways should be explored. Such mechanisms 
would allow technical and medical experts to contribute meaningfully to 
governance, while still advancing in their professions. This approach would 
ensure that the nation’s human capital is not only preserved but fully optimised.  
The Committee reiterates  DoPT to establish a clear timeline for implementation 
of the Baswan Commi ttee’s reforms by  forming a dedicated team to monitor 
progress in the direction of  exam restructuring. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.8 The Committee appreciates the UPSC and SSC for conducting the diligence 
exercises before publishing the answer keys. Howe ver, the Committee is of the 
view that this will become further more credible if the feedback of the candidates 
are taken through a dedicated portal and then keys are published. The Committee 
hopes that this process will be followed in future. Further, UPSC should explore the 
feasibility of declaring the answer key of Civil Services Preliminary exams after the 
Preliminary Exam stage is over and not after the declaration of final results of the 
Civil Services examination. Candidates should be allowed to raise objections at this 
stage only and on that basis any discrepancies related to the answer key of the 
Preliminary examination should be resolved.   This should be taken into account 
before publishing the result of candidates qualifying for the next stage, i. e. Civil 
Services Mains examination. (Para 2.39) 
Action Taken  
3.9 Union Public Service Commission (UPSC)  is already having an online 
Question Paper Representation Portal (QPRep ) in its website where candidates can 
submit their views on any aspect of a question. This portal remains active for an 
exam for a period of 7 days from the next date immediately after the conclusion of 
that exam. In respect of the release of the answer ke y, it is stated that the 
Commission releases the answer key of the Civil Services (Preliminary) 

59 
 
Examination (objective type) after completion of the entire process of the Civil 
Services Examination. This policy of the Commission is being followed in all 
Examinations of the Commission and it has been working smoothly. Further, 
candidates can make representations on the questions through the dedicated portal, 
as explained above.  As the above system of disclosing keys after the final result of 
the Examination  is working fine since inception and serving the larger public 
interest very well, no requirement is felt to change the same. Further, the issue of 
releasing answer keys is presently sub -judice in W.P. No. 8626/2023 filed by Shri 
Himanshu and others vs  UPSC & Others before the Hon’ble Delhi High Court. 
This case was last heard on 01.12.2023 and listed for next hearing on 21.05.2024. 
3.10 Staff Selection Commission (SSC)  has informed that   in order to ensure 
greater transparency in the examination - system, and in the interest of the 
candidates, the SSC already as the following process in the place: - (i) The tentative 
answer keys of all computer based examinations are uploaded on the Commission’s 
website soon after the conduct of the examination, affordin g the candidates with an 
opportunity to make representations/ challenges against discrepancies, if any, in 
Question Paper/ Tentative Answer Keys.; (ii) On receipt of the challenges, the 
Commission, through a panel of experts, exercises due diligence before  preparing 
the Final Answer keys. Thereafter, the result is declared on the basis of the Final 
Answer keys. The Final answer keys are also uploaded on the website of the 
Commission whereby the candidates are able to judge their performance in the 
examinations.; (iii) Marks secured by the candidates in various examinations 
conducted by the commission are also hosted on website for the information of 
individual candidates. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.11 The Committee recommends that UPSC consider establishing a 
dedicated portal for collecting candidate feedback and objections on the 
provisional answer keys of the Preliminary Examination. It should aim to 
release these keys soon after the exam, following S SC’s transparent model, 
and provide a clear window of 7 to 10 days for raising objections. An expert 
panel should review all submissions before Mains results are announced, and 
final corrected answer keys should be published to help candidates understand 
the evaluation process. Additionally, UPSC and SSC must ensure that all 
related communication is timely and widely disseminated through official 
channels to keep all candidates informed. A uniform, standardised policy for 
handling answer keys across all UPS C examinations may be adopted for 

60 
 
clarity and consistency. The Committee also suggests that UPSC consider the 
outcome of the ongoing court case on this issue and review its approach 
accordingly. Benchmarking these practices against those of global public 
service commissions could further strengthen fairness and credibility. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.12 With respect to Railway Recruitment Board, the Committee emphasized that 
number of centers have to be increased for the candidates appearing for the 
examination. The examination centre should be within the zone where the 
candidate is residing, precisely within the State. (Para 2.52) 
Action Taken  
3.13 Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) conduct examination covering 
different Geographical locations/ States all over the country even as far as all seven 
North-East States, Islands of Andaman & Nicobar as well as Lakshadweep &  
Kashmir valley in north. Due to large number of candidates i.e. more than one 
crore, it is not always possible to allot centres near the pla ce of residence of the 
candidates. However, in allotting of centre it is ensured that Persons with 
Benchmark Disabilities (PwBD) & female candidates are allotted centres near their 
residence. In the recent examinations to avoid long distance travel, it was  decided 
that as far as possible no candidates should travel more than 500 kilometers.  A 
massive recruitment exercise has been completed recently for empaneling 1,39,050 
candidates by conducting Computer Based Test (CBT) of approximately 2.37 crore 
candidates. CBT for Centralized Employment Notification (CEN) 01/2019 for Non-
Technical Popular Categories (NTPC) was conducted for 1.26 crore candidates in 
133 shifts in 68 days across 211 cities and 726 centres in 15 languages. Similarly, 
CBT for CEN-RRC 01/2019 (Level-1) was conducted for 1.11 crore candidates in 
99 shifts in 33 days across 191 cities and 551 centres in 15 languages. These 
processes were carried out with absolute fairness and transparency. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.14 The Committee acknowledges the immense scale and effort involved in 
conducting examinations for large numbers of candidates across diverse 
regions; however, it stresses the need to further expand the number of 
examination centres, with a focus on allotting  centres within a candidate’s State 
or zone of residence wherever possible. While it appreciates the special 
provisions for PwBD and female candidates, the Committee recommends 

61 
 
extending similar consideration to all candidates, particularly those from rura l 
or remote areas, to reduce travel burdens. It also suggests that RRBs consider 
adopting a zonal preference -based allocation system during the application 
process. The Commission further recommends improved coordination with local 
authorities and private infrastructure providers to identify additional venues. 
These measures would not only ease logistical challenges but also  lower travel 
expenses, and promote equitable access to the recruitment process across all 
regions.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3.15 The Committee advocates to examine the following in details by IBPS. 
(i)    An assessment of the cost for an applicant to reach to the 
examination centre from his house and pay the fee.   
(ii)      The strike rate for a candidate to get a job.   
(iii)      An assessment of the cost of an unemployed person to only apply 
and not get the job.   
(iv) The Committee notes that on an average approximately 95 per 
cent of the candidates who apply are not able to get selected and left 
without job. However, every one is being charged and mostly they are 
unemployed.  Hence, the Committee recommends that it would be fair 
and can be explored that the State or the Central Government bear part of 
that cost so that it does not burden the unemployed youth.  (Para 2.76)  
Action Taken  
3.16 With respect to Point (i) to (iv), Department of Financial Services has 
furnished following information/inputs 
i. Noted for information 
ii. It is at about 0.75%, as number of vacancies are less as compared 
to number of applicants competing. 
iii. Noted for examination 
iv. At present, no such proposal exists. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.17 The Committee notes the limited response from the Department and urges 
that a more detailed and structured study be undertaken by IBPS, in 
coordination with the Department of Financial Services, to assess the financial 

62 
 
burden borne by unemployed youth who apply for competitive examinations but 
do not secure employment. In light of the extremely low strike rate of around 
0.75% and the fact that nearly all ap plicants, many of whom are unemployed, 
are charged examination fees and incur significant travel and other related 
expenses, the Committee reiterates its recommendation that the Government  
may explore mechanisms to subsidise a portion of these costs. This could be done 
through direct financial assistance, fee waivers for certain categories, or 
establishing a common subsidy framework for unemployed candidates 
appearing in public recruitment processes. Such measures would reflect a more 
empathetic and inclusive approach to support  youth in their efforts to secure 
gainful employment and reduce the financial strain on economically vulnerable 
applicants. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.18 The Committee notes the travelling undertaken by the candidates to appear in 
the examination and advises RRBs and IBPS to analyze and assess from which 
areas they get a large number of applications. If from a particular State or area they 
are getting a large number of applications, then contemplate increasing the number 
of centers in that area so that the agencies which are being hired for conducting 
exams set up more centers. It should be planned in such a way that it would be 
convenient for candidates. They should not travel more than 100 kms. or 200 kms. 
Also, for candidates who are travelling from far away distances to sit in the 
examinations, it should be ensured that measures are taken to make the travel more 
humane and comfortable. Some special trains  may be run for the purpose. The 
Committee feels these measures would ease the burden of the candidates. (Para 
2.77) 
Action Taken  
3.19 Department of Financial Services  has informed that IBPS deci des upon the 
number of centers/ venues in any particular State according to the number of 
candidates expected in the examination, and endeavors to provide candidates their 
choice of center as close to their opted city as possible. If number from a particular 
area is larger than expected,  new centers are added. Even in relatively very 
inaccessible areas (e.g., Lakshadweep), test center is provided regardless of very 
low number of candidates. The number of grievances of candidates in this regard is 
minimal. 

63 
 
3.20 Railway Recruitment Boards (RRBs) conduct examination covering different 
Geographical locations/ States all over the country even as far as all seven North -
East States, Islands of Andaman & Nicobar as well as Lakshadweep & Kashmir 
valley in north. Due to large number of candidates i.e. more than one crore, it is not 
always possible to allot centres near the place of residence of the candidates. 
However, in allotting of centre it is ensured that Persons with Benchmark 
Disabilities (PwBD) & female candidates are allotted centres near th eir residence. 
In the recent examinations to avoid long distance travel, it was decided that as far 
as possible no candidates should travel more than 500 kilometers. Moreover, 
Special Trains are operated as per requirements for ease of candidates. 
Further Recommendation/Observation 
3.21 The Committee appreciates the efforts of IBPS and RRBs in expanding 
access of examination centres, including to remote and low -applicant areas. 
However, a more data -driven and proactive approach is needed. Recruitment 
agencies should identify high -application-density regions in advance and plan 
additional centres accordingly. This will help  in ensuring that candidates travel 
less than 100 kilometres for exams.  The Committee stresses the importance of 
making the process more candidate -friendly, especially for those from rural, 
remote, and economically weaker sections. It also recommends special transport 
arrangements—such as reserved coaches or special trains—in coordination with 
Indian Railways and State Transport Authorities. These should be planned well 
ahead of major exam dates. Information about such services must be widely 
publicised to help candidates plan their travel, reduce stress, and lower costs. 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.22 The Committee suggests that a standard feedback module be prepared by the 
organizations which are responsible for conduct of the examinations. Once the 
students have completed the examination cycle, they may be given an option to fill 
in this standardized module. This module may contain various heads like syllabus, 
time taken to complete the exam, constraints faced, infrastructure issues like 
internet connectivity etc, logistical issu es and so on. This will help the 
organizations make the recruitm ent cycle even more streamlined and fast . (Para 
2.104) 
  

64 
 
Action Taken  
3.23 `Feedback' module is available on the webpage of the UPSC 
(i.e. https://www.upsc.gov.in), where  any person can record his/her views/ 
comments/ suggestions in respect of any examination of the Commission including 
the CAPF(AC) Examination, which is conducted by the Commission for 
recruitment to the posts of Assistant Commandants in CAPFs. This feedba ck 
window remains available on 24 X 7 basis. Further, the people can also make 
representation through emails and other modes as they deem appropriate.  
3.24 Staff Selection Commission follows a transparent system of examination and 
continuous feedback of t he examinees is an integral part of the system. As part of 
the process of the examination system, the answer keys of the questions are 
finalized after getting due feedback from the candidates. Continuous feedback is 
also received in the form of representations/ grievances/ other references etc. These 
inputs are considered and appropriate measures taken. Based on such feedback, the 
Commission has started the practice of providing a window for correction of online 
application forms. This has enabled the candi dates to rectify the mistakes, if any, 
committed by them during the filling up of online applications. 
Further Recommendations/ Observations 
3.25 The Committee appreciates the existing feedback mechanisms of both 
UPSC and SSC . However, it  recommends a uniform, structured feedback 
module for all recruitment agencies, including UPSC, SSC, IBPS, and RRBs. 
This module should be mandatory at the end of each examination cycle and 
cover aspects such as syllabus relevance, question design, time ma nagement, 
infrastructure issues, language options, accessibility, logistics, and other 
constraints. Feedback should be collected in a consistent, analyzable format to 
enable regular assessment and improvement and the data should be periodically 
reviewed to enhance transparency and demonstrate responsiveness. A uniform 
framework would help identify systemic issues, improve the candidate 
experience, and streamline the recruitment process . The Committee also 
recommends that, in the event of an abrupt cancellat ion of an examination due 
to technical or procedural issues, appropriate steps should be taken to conduct a 
re-examination within three months, in the interest of the aspirants.

CHAPTER - IV 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH 
FINAL REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
4.0 The Committee wants to know about the feedback mechanism and suggestions 
of candidates taking civil services and other examinations. Also, whether UPSC and 
SSC publish the key of civ il services preliminary examination before finalizing the 
result of prelims and selecting candidates for Mains. Whether UPSC invites 
objections from candidates and reviews the key before finalizing the result of 
preliminary examination. (Para 2.34) 
4.1 The Committee emphasizes on filling up of all vacancies on mission mode in 
consonance with the Government’s policy. The Committee recommends that there

R E P O R T 
  
 This Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the action taken by the Legislative 
Department (Ministry of Law and Justice) on the Recommendations/ Observations of the 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and 
Justice in its One Hundred and Forty Nine (149th) Report of the Committee on Demands for Grants 
(2025-26) of the Legislative Department (Ministry of Law and Justice), which was presented to the 
Rajya Sabha on 27th March, 2025 and laid on the Table of the Lok Sabha on the 27th March, 2025. 
2. The Committee had made 11 recommendations/observations in its 149th    Report. Replies of 
the Department thereto have been categorized and scrutinized under four chapters on the basis of 
satisfaction of the Committee. These replies have been categorized as follows: 
Chapter – I: Recommendations/observations which have been accepted by the Ministry: 
Para:- 2.20 (Total- 01). 
Chapter – II:   Recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue 
in view of the replies given by the Ministry: Paras:- 2.35 and 2.38 (Total-02).  
Chapter – III:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which Committee has not accepted 
the replies of the Ministry: Paras:- 2.21, 2.22, 2.27 and 2.36 (Total-04). 
Chapter – IV:   Recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry 
have not been received by the Committee: Paras:- 3.5, 3.6, 3.10 and 3.11  
(Total-04).  
3. The Committee desires that the Department should furnish pointed and detailed Action 
Taken Notes in respect of all the further Recommendations/Observations made by the Committee in 
Chapter – III of this report. 
4. The details of the ATR have been discussed in the respective Chapters in the succeeding 
pages. For reference purpose, para numbers of the original report (i.e. of 149th Report) have been 
mentioned at the end of each Recommendation/Observation.   
  

2 
 
CHAPTER I 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1.1 The Committee observes that the Department has been able to spend about 80% of the RE 
(2024-25) upto 31st January, 2025. The Committee appreciates the Department for incurring the 
expenditure uniformly as a whole till 31st January, 2025 keeping in view the instructions issued by 
the Ministry of Finance (MoF), wherein the expenditure in the last quarter has to be restricted to 
33% ceiling and in last month (March) expenditure has to be restricted to 15% of ceiling. The 
Committee hopes that the Department shall strive to utilize the budget uniformly in the remaining 
part of FY 2024-25 and in forthcoming financial year 2025-26.             (Para 2.20)  
 
Action Taken 
 
1.2 Recommendations/ observations made by the Committee have been noted for future 
compliance. The Legislative Department will put in its best efforts to comply with the prescribed 
ceilings of expenditure per quarter/month of the financial year, as provided by the Department of 
Expenditure, Ministry of Finance.

CHAPTER II 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT 
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE REPLIES GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.1  The Committee in its previous reports, 101st, 107th, 114th and 130th reports on Demands for 
Grants suggested the Department to take the work related to translation of the Constitution in 
scheduled languages on priority. The Committee also observes that translation work have been 
done upto 106th Amendment in Hindi, Maithili, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Sanskrit and Urdu 
this year, as the updation work upto 105th amendment was done till the last Demands for Grants. 
However, so far 106 Amendments have taken place.               (Para 2.35) 
Action Taken 
 
2.2 As regards the Committee’s observation, it is submitted that besides Hindi, Maithili, 
Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Sanskrit and Urdu, the Constitution of India is updated up to 106th 
Amendment in Kashmiri language also. The publication of updated version of the Constitution of 
India in Telugu is ready to be published soon. The Central Institute of Indian Languages has been 
assigned the work of translation and updation of the Constitution of India in Assamese, Bodo, 
Gujarati, Konkani, Nepali, Odia, Santhali and Sindhi, and the work is under process. This 
Department is making all efforts to speed up the updation and translation of the Constitution of 
India in Bengali, Dogri, Kannada, Manipuri and Tamil languages, with the cooperation of 
respective State Governments. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
2.3 As far as repealing of Obsolete laws is concerned, the Committee appreciates the work done 
in this regard and that 1824 redundant and obsolete laws have been identified to be repealed. The 
Committee also feels that the laws prevalent in a country should be representative of the political 
and social structure existing at that time. The Committee hopes that the department will undertake 
such exercise of identifying and repealing the obsolete laws on regular and continuous basis in 
future also.                    (Para 2.38) 
 

4 
 
 
Action Taken 
 
2.4 As regards the Committee’s observation, it is stated that the present Government, as part of 
its resolve to bring reforms in the legal system had constituted a two Member Committee in 2014 to 
undertake comprehensive review of laws with a view to remove obsolete and redundant laws. On 
the basis of the recommendations of the said Two Member Committee and the Law Commission, 
the Legislative Department had identified 1824 redundant and obsolete Acts. After due examination 
and consultations with concerned Ministries and Department, a total of 1562 Central Acts have 
since been repealed through various Repealing and Amending Acts, Finance and Income Tax Acts. 
Apart from this 14 more pre-constitution Acts have been repealed through various Acts. Further, as 
different Ministries and Department are allocated different subject Matters, this Department has, 
vide its various D.O. letters, time and again requested all Ministries/Departments to take immediate 
necessary action to ensure the obsolete laws administered by them are repealed or re-enacted if so 
required as expeditiously as possible. Further, the Twenty-third Law Commission of India has been 
constituted with a mandate inter alia to examine review/repeal of obsolete laws.

CHAPTER III 
 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE 
DOES NOT ACCEPT THE REASONS GIVEN BY THE MINISTRY AND REITERATES 
ITS RECOMMENDATION 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.1  The Committee observes that huge reductions in allocations in BE (2025-26) over the 
projections made to the Ministry of Finance for the year 2025-26 under various heads have been 
done, namely Legislative Department (about 36%), Official Language Wing(OLW) (about 61%) 
and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (about 27%) on the revenue Side and EVMs for Election Commission 
(about 94%), Official Language Wing(OLW) (about 158%), Legislative Department (about 386%) 
and Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (about 272%) on the Capital Side. The Committee is not aware about 
the reasons for such major reductions under various heads. The Committee feels that the 
Department is failing on its part to seek realistic financial projection targets from the Ministry of 
Finance which may be due to its inaccurate projection or inflation of funds. The Committee is, 
therefore, of the view the department should improve its financial forecasting methods using past 
expenditure trends to prevent such large discrepancies between its projections and actual 
allocations. Further, the department should engage with the Ministry of Finance (MoF) regularly to 
avoid budget cuts.                     (Para 2.21) 
 
Action Taken

Further Recommendation/Observation: 
3.8 The Committee reiterates that the Department should take proactive measures to 
ensure timely utilization of funds allocated for procurement of EVMs and VVPATs. While the 
Committee notes that procedural delays due to non-receipt of invoices from manufacturers 
were cited as reasons, it emphasizes the need for better coordination with the Election 
Commission of India and the manufacturers to avoid such delays in future. The Committee 
further recommends that the Department should develop a monitoring mechanism to track 
fund utilization and procurement schedules on a quarterly basis. 
Recommendation/Observation  
 
3.9  The Committee observes that the number of vacancies in the Legislative Department has 
increased over a period of time. Despite the recommendations of the Committee in its earlier 
reports regarding the filling of vacancies, it seems that the Department is not giving a thought to fill 
up the vacancies as it has been furnishing vague and routine replies. Therefore, the Committee 
recommends that the department should coordinate with the recruitment agencies continuously to 
fill up all the required vacancies so that the work of it is not hampered in terms of the assigned 
mandate. Further, the Department may consider hiring through outsourcing until permanent staff is 
recruited and also, expedite the amendments in RRs to remove outdated criteria hindering 
recruitment.                         (Para 2.27)

3.15  The Committee, accordingly, recommends that the work related to translation and updation 
of the Constitution of India in all the Scheduled languages of the Constitution be expedited. The 
Committee, further, recommends that a policy framework or a legal mandate may be introduced by 
the Department to ensure that every constitutional amendment is translated within a fixed 
timeframe in all scheduled languages. Further, the feasibility of outsourcing a part of the 
translation work to certified language experts or universities specializing in regional languages 
may be explored.                   (Para 2.36)  
 
Action Taken 
 
3.16 As regards the Committee’s observation, it is submitted that there is already a constitutional 
mandate on the part of the Department to make available the Constitution of India in Regional 
Languages and the Regional Languages Unit. Official Language Wing is making all efforts to 
expedite the translation and updation work of the Constitution of India in all Languages enshrined 
in the 8th Schedule to the Constitution of India, i.e., Assamese, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, 
Malayalam, Marathi, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, Urdu, Sanskrit, Sindhi, Kashmiri, Nepali, 
Manipuri, Dogri, Bodo, Santhali, Maithili and Konkani. With the cooperation of the concerned 
State Governments, efforts are being made to update the Indian Constitution into the respective 
language within the time frame.  
  
3.17 It is also mentioned that the translation of Constitution of India in the respective language is 
provided by the concerned State Governments. For the languages for which no officer is available 
in Regional Languages Unit, the Department has entrusted the work of updation and translation to 
the Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL), a government organisation under the aegis of 
Ministry of Education. The translation of any statute or law should be done by the person who are 
expert in legal language. Every State Government has a Directorate of Language and Commission, 

11 
 
who have their own infrastructure with reference to printing, publication and experts of legal 
language for translation. Hence, it is not feasible to outsource translation work to language experts 
or Universities.   
 
Further Recommendation/Observation: 
3.18 The Committee notes the submission of the Ministry that outsourcing the translation 
work to language experts or universities may not be feasible due to administrative and 
procedural constraints. However, the Committee emphasizes that the timely translation of 
every Constitutional Amendment is of utmost importance to ensure consistency and 
accessibility of legal texts in all official languages. Therefore, it recommends that the 
Department should explore and adopt an effective alternative mechanism, to ensure that all 
translation work is completed within the fixed timeframe.

CHAPTER - IV 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH FINAL 
REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY HAVE NOT BEEN RECEIVED 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.1 It is also observed that out of the total allocation of Rs 361.76 crore in RE(2024-25), Rs 
268.34 crore has been spent upto 31st January, 2025, which is approximately 74 percent of RE 
(2024-25). The Committee appreciates the Commission for incurring the expenditure uniformly as a 
whole till 31st January, 2025 keeping in view the instructions issued by the Ministry of Finance 
(MoF), wherein the expenditure in the last quarter has to be restricted to 33% ceiling and in last 
month (March) expenditure has to be restricted to 15% of ceiling. The Committee hopes that the 
Commission will be able to utilize the remaining budget for the remaining part of Financial year 
2024-25 uniformily.                            (Para 3.5)  
4.2 However, the Committee, also observes that out of the total allocation of Rs. 27.91 crore in 
RE (2024-25) under the Capital head, the commission has been able to spent only Rs. 3.93 crore 
upto 31st January, 2025 which is about 14 percent of the RE (2024-25). The Committee fails to 
understand the reason behind such under-utilization of funds. Low capital expenditure utilization 
(14% of RE 2024-25 spent as of 31st January, 2025) indicates either inefficiencies in fund 
deployment or delays in procurement. Accordingly, the Committee recommends the ECI to improve 
its spending capacity on its capital side and ensure timely utilization of allocated capital funds, as 
non- expenditure tantamount to under-utilisation of resources.                   (Para 3.6) 
4.3 The Committee observes that out of the total 850 post, 275 posts are vacant which is about 
32% of the total sanctioned strength. The Committee shows its concern as a large number of 
vacancies still exist, especially at the level of Assistant Section Officer, Senior Secretariat Assistant, 
Steno Grade 'D', Junior Secretariat Assistant, MTS which is hampering its working. The vacancies 
in the Commission have accumulated over a period of time and accordingly, recommends the 
Commission to expedite the process of recruitment.                    (Para 3.10) 
4.4 The Committee is given to understand that whenever the elections are announced in states, 
the Model Code of Conduct comes into place immediately on announcement and trade gets hit. 
Though, Digital transactions have made a huge impact, still a large portion of the country’s 
economy is cash economy. In the pretext of implementation of the Model Code of Conduct, even the 

13 
 
genuine transactions of the traders are seized which impacts the trader and the economy. The 
Committee desires that ECI should have a mechanism to verify the purpose for which the money is 
being transacted. On verification, if it is found to be for legal purpose, then the entire money should 
be released immediately.                       (Para 3.11)  
Further Recommendation/Observation:  
4.5  The Committee has not received replies to recommendations of the Committee of the 
above paras i.e., 3.5, 3.6, 3.10 and 3.11 from the Legislative Department/Election Commission.  
The Committee would like to remind the Department that Action taken Replies should be 
furnished before the Committee within three months from the day when Report on Demands 
for Grants is presented in Parliament.
