uptime. It will help in timely implementation of this feature. 
(Para 2.123) 
 
30. The Committee is of the view that, in designing the AI-powered Multimodal 
Multilingual Assistant and NextGen CPGRAMS, the Department provide 
comprehensive accessibility features, including voice-based interaction, simplified 
interfaces for low-literacy users, Divyangjan-friendly design, and the capability to 
upload photographs, videos and documents, while ensuring robust data security and 
privacy safeguards. 
(Para 2.124) 
 
 
31. The Committee recommends that the Department, in consultation with State 
Governments and Administrative Training Institutes (ATIs), prepare a time-bound 
Capacity Building Action Plan with quantified annual targets for training officers at 
State, district and sub district levels, ensuring coverage of all major service-delivery 
Departments and mandatory orientation on NextGen CPGRAMS features. 
(Para 2.136) 
***** 
Department of Pensions and Pensioners’ Welfare 
 
Budget Analysis of DPPW 
32. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Pension and 
Pensioners’ Welfare, in coordination with the Ministry of Personnel, Public Grievances 
and Pensions and the other concerned Ministry, take expeditious steps to relocate its 
offices to suitable Government-owned premises, wherever feasible, instead of continuing 
in rented accommodation. Such relocation would result in substantial savings to the 
public exchequer by eliminating recurring rental expenditure. 
(Para 3.6) 
 
33. Under Object Head 05.03.28 – Professional Services, the Committee observes a 
sharp and disproportionate increase in allocation during the financial year 2025–26. 
The Budget Estimate remained at ₹12 lakh during the financial years 2023–24 and 
2024–25, whereas it increased sharply to ₹3.00 crore during 2025–26. However, actual 
expenditure as on 13 January 2026 stood at only ₹1.03 crore. The Committee notes that 
this significant gap between allocation and actual utilization (34.33 percent only) 
indicates overestimation of requirements and inadequate expenditure planning. 
                              (Para 3.7) 

 
54 
 
34. Under Object Head 05.03.31 – Grants-in-Aid, the Committee notes that the 
Budget Estimate for the financial year 2025–26 was ₹3.00 crore, which was reduced to 
₹1.00 crore at the Revised Estimates stage, while actual expenditure was only ₹10.50 
lakh as on 13 January 2026. The Committee is concerned that such low utilization of 
funds (3.5 per cent only) allocated for welfare-related activities adversely affects 
implementation of pensioners’ welfare programmes.     
                                                                                                               (Para 3.8) 
 
35. The Committee, in view of the above observations, recommends that the 
Department strengthen its budget estimation and financial planning processes to ensure 
realistic projections and avoiding large variations between Budget Estimates, Revised 
Estimates and Actual Expenditure, particularly under Object Heads 05.03.27 (Minor 
Works), 05.03.28 (Professional Services), and 05.03.31 (Grants-in-Aid). 
(Para 3.9) 
 
36. The Committee also recommends strengthening internal financial monitoring 
systems to ensure timely and optimal utilization of allocated funds and to prevent 
avoidable under-utilisation of resources. 
(Para 3.10) 
 
Policies, Programmes and Schemes of DPPW 
37. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department undertake targeted 
and inclusive awareness campaigns specifically aimed at vulnerable and special 
categories of pensioners, including retired artisans, elderly pensioners, and pensioners 
residing in remote and rural areas. These awareness initiatives should focus on 
educating pensioners about the mandatory requirement of submitting Digital Life 
Certificates, the timelines involved, and the various available methods for submitting 
DLC, including face authentication, mobile-based submission, and assisted modes. 
(Para 3.14) 
 
38. The Committee further suggests that such awareness campaigns be conducted 
through multiple outreach channels, including pensioner welfare associations, Common 
Service Centres (CSCs), banks, post offices, local administrative offices and field-level 
functionaries. Special assistance mechanisms may also be established to facilitate 
submission of DLC for pensioners with limited digital access or mobility constraints. 
(Para 3.15) 
 
39. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department undertake a 
detailed analysis of the nature and categories of the annual pension-related complaints 
received through CPENGRAMS, with a view to identifying recurring issues, procedural 
bottlenecks, and systemic deficiencies contributing to grievance generation. The 
Committee further recommends that the Department implement appropriate systemic 
reforms, including process simplification, strengthening of digital pension processing 
systems, capacity building of dealing officials, and enhanced monitoring mechanisms, in 
order to reduce grievance generation at source.           
                                                        (Para 3.19) 

 
55 
 
40. The Committee notes that Pension Adalats serve as an important institutional 
mechanism for expeditious and on-the-spot resolution of pension-related grievances. 
However, the effectiveness of such Adalats depends significantly on the extent to which 
pensioners are made aware of these opportunities in advance. The Committee is of the 
view that lack of timely and adequate dissemination of information may prevent many 
eligible pensioners, particularly those residing in remote areas or those with limited 
digital access, from availing themselves of this grievance redressal mechanism. 
                                                                                                                        (Para 3.22) 
 
41. The Committee emphasises the need for the Department to undertake 
widespread and well-coordinated awareness campaigns sufficiently in advance of 
organising Pension Adalats, so as to ensure that all pensioners with pending grievances 
are informed and able to participate. Information regarding Pension Adalats should be 
disseminated through multiple channels, including pensioner welfare associations, 
pension disbursing banks, post offices, and relevant Government offices, in addition to 
digital platforms such as official websites, pension portals, SMS alerts, and social media. 
(Para 3.23) 
 
 
42. The Committee recommends that the Department strengthen the Anubhav 
Awards scheme by giving it wider publicity across all Ministries/Departments and their 
attached/subordinate offices and by examining the feasibility of providing appropriate 
monetary incentives or enhanced cash awards to Anubhav awardees and selected 
contributors. 
(Para 3.26) 
 
43. The Committee recommends that the Department develop and implement a 
centralised digital clearance mechanism through a dedicated online portal, integrated 
with existing pension processing systems, to enable retiring employees to obtain all 
required No Objection Certificates (NOCs) electronically. The portal should 
automatically route clearance requests to all concerned offices, provide real-time status 
tracking, and ensure electronic issuance of NOCs in a time-bound manner.  
(Para 3.31) 
 
 
44. The Committee is of the view that such a digital and 55entralized system would 
enhance transparency, improve administrative efficiency, prevent delays in settlement 
of retirement benefits, and significantly reduce hardship faced by retiring employees, 
while aligning with the Government’s objective of strengthening digital governance. 
(Para 3.32) 
 
45. The Committee recommends that the Department expedite efforts to achieve 100 
per cent integration by onboarding the remaining banks at the earliest, ensuring 
comprehensive digital access to pension services for all beneficiaries. 
(Para 3.34) 
 

 
56 
46. The Committee recommend that, in view of the alarming increase in cyber 
frauds and online financial scams, the Department of Pension and Pensioners’ Welfare 
should design and implement targeted cyber-security and fraud-prevention awareness 
campaigns for Government pensioners and family pensioners, in coordination with 
banks, India Post Payments Bank, Common Service Centres and Pensioners’ Welfare 
Associations, so as to sensitise them against sharing OTPs/passwords, how to identify 
and respond to fake “pension verification” calls or links, and to apprise them of 
available mechanisms for reporting such incidents. 
(Para 3.37) 
 
47. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department consider 
introducing a Welfare Inspector system, on the lines of the model implemented in the 
Railway Department, to provide dedicated assistance and facilitation to retiring 
employees and pensioners. The Committee is of the view that Welfare Inspectors may 
be designated to function as nodal facilitators to guide retiring employees through all 
stages of retirement and pension processing. 
(Para 3.41) 
 
 
 
48. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department undertake a 
comprehensive study and detailed assessment to ascertain the reasons for the limited 
response to migration from NPS to UPS. The study should identify key barriers, 
procedural constraints, lack of awareness, or any perceived disadvantages or 
disincentives associated with the scheme. 
(Para 3.46) 
 
49. The Committee welcomes these initiatives and appreciates the efforts made by 
the Department in this regard. 
(Para 3.56)

DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE 
 
Functions of the Department 
 
1.4 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, functions of the 
Department are as under: 
 
i. Appointment, resignation and removal of the Chief Justice of India and Judges 
of the Supreme Court of India; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of 
absence (including leave allowance), pensions and travelling allowances; 
ii. Appointment, resignation and removal etc. of Chief Justice and Judges of 
High Courts in States; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence 
(including leave allowances), pensions and travelling allowances; 
iii. Appointment of Judicial Commissioners and Judicial Officers in Union 
Territories; 
iv. Constitution and organization (excluding jurisdiction and powers) of the 
Supreme Court (but including contempt of such Court) and the fees taken 
therein; 
v. Constitution and organization of the High Courts and the Courts of Judicial 
Commissioners except provisions as to officers and servants of these Courts; 
vi. Administration of justice and constitution and organization of Courts in the 
Union Territories and fees taken in such Courts; 
vii. Courts fees and Stamp duties in the Union Territories; 
viii. Creation of All India Judicial Service; 
ix. Conditions of service of District Judges and other Members of Higher Judicial 
Service of Union Territories; 
x. Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory or exclusion 
of a Union Territory from the Jurisdiction of a High Court; 
xi. Legal Aid to the poor; 
xii. Administration of Justice; and 
xiii. Access to Justice, Justice Delivery and Legal Reforms. 
 
OVERALL ASSESSMENT OF THE DEMANDS FOR GRANTS  
 
1.5 The Demands for Grants for the financial year 2026-27 of the Ministry of Law and 
Justice was presented to the Parliament under Demand No. 65.  The Department-related

 1.14 The primary responsibility for development of judicial infrastructure in the States 
rests with the State Governments.  The Central Government augments the resources of the 
State Governments by providing financial assistance under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme 
(CSS) for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judiciary. The Centrally 

 
8 
Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for development of infrastructure facilities for Judiciary is being 
implemented since 1993-94. Under this scheme, the Central Government augments the 
resources of the State Governments by providing financial assistance in prescribed fund 
sharing pattern i.e. 60:40 (Centre: State); (90:10 for the North-Eastern and 2 Himalayan 
States) and 100% for UTs.

Centrally Sponsored Scheme for Development of Infrastructure Facilities for the Judiciary for 
the period 2021–22 to 2025–26 on 14 July 2021 with an outlay of ₹9,000 crore, including a 
Central share of ₹5,357 crore (₹50 crore earmarked for Gram Nyayalayas), that the Scheme 
now also covers construction of Lawyers’ Halls, Toilet Complexes and Digital Computer

1.17 On analysing the above Table, it is observed that a total of 2,171 Court Halls and 
1,333 Residential Units have been completed across States and Union Territories during the 
period 2021-22 to 2025-26 (as on 31.01.2026) The data indicates wide inter-State variation in 
the pace and scale of infrastructure creation. States such as Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya 
Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan and Bihar account for a substantial share of completed 

 
11 
Court Halls, reflecting relatively better utilisation of funds and implementation capacity. In 
contrast, several States and Union Territories, including Arunachal Pradesh, Manipur, 
Nagaland, Lakshadweep, Ladakh and certain UTs, have reported negligible or nil completion 
during the period, pointing to persistent regional imbalances. 
 
1.18 In their written submission, the Department highlighted several problems affecting the 
implementation of the Scheme, including slow pace of expenditure, inadequate monitoring at 
the State level, procedural delays, delays in submission of e-payment files, law and order 
issues in certain States, limited working seasons, and challenges arising from the transition to 
the SNA-SPARSH model. 
1.19 During the course of examination of the Demands for Grants (DFG) for 2026–27, the 
Committee observed that many courts, especially High Courts and subordinate courts, do not 
have adequate basic facilities. The Committee noted that court buildings are often 
overcrowded and lack proper seating, sanitation, ventilation and other essential amenities for 
judges, lawyers and litigants. The Committee also observed that suitable facilities for women 
lawyers, including dedicated spaces and child-care or crèche facilities, are generally not 
available. In addition, the Committee noted shortcomings in digital infrastructure, such as 
poor internet connectivity and Wi-Fi facilities, which affect the effective functioning of e-
Courts. The Committee further observed that while better facilities are available in the 
Supreme Court of India, similar facilities have not been provided uniformly across High 
Courts and subordinate courts. 
1.20 The Committee notes that the Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for 
Development of Infrastructure Facilities for Judiciary has played a significant role in 
augmenting judicial infrastructure across the States and Union Territories, as reflected 
in the cumulative release of Central assistance and the creation of Court halls and 
residential units. However, the Committee expresses concern over the slow pace of 
expenditure and utilisation of funds in several States during 2025–26, despite 
substantial releases made under the Scheme. 
1.21 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department in coordination 
with the State Governments and High Court Level Monitoring Committees, strengthen 
monitoring and review mechanisms to ensure timely utilisation of funds and completion 
of projects. The Committee also recommends that the Department take proactive 
measures to address procedural and system-related bottlenecks, including capacity 
building for effective implementation of the SNA-SPARSH framework, so that the 
objectives of the Scheme are achieved. 

 
12 
1.22 The Committee further recommends that the Department, in coordination with 
the judicial authorities and State Governments, take time-bound measures to upgrade 
court infrastructure across the country. The Committee emphasises the need for 
gender-sensitive court design, including provision of separate and adequate facilities for 
women lawyers, litigants and staff, as well as dedicated child-care and crèche facilities 
within court complexes. The Committee further recommends that deficiencies in digital 
infrastructure and the non-availability of proper network connectivity in courts be 
urgently addressed. The Committee also stress that such facilities should be uniformly 
extended to High Courts and subordinate courts, and not remain confined only to the 
Supreme Court of India.

1.21 The Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 came into force with effect from 2nd October, 2009. 
The Act provides for the establishment of Gram Nyayalayas at intermediate Panchayat level 
for the purpose of providing access to justice to the citizens at their doorstep. In terms of 
Section 3(1) of the Gram Nyayalayas Act, State Governments, after consultation with the 
High Court concerned, may, by notification, establish one or two more Gram Nyayalayas for 
every Panchayat at intermediate level or a group of contiguous Panchayats at intermediate 
level in a district or where there is no Panchayat at intermediate level in any State, for a group 
of contiguous group Panchayats. Establishment of Gram Nyayalayas is, therefore, not 
mandatory on the part of State Governments as per the Act. However, the State Governments 
are requested from time to time to establish Gram Nyayalayas. Till date 488 Gram 
Nyayalayas have been notified by 15 States, out of which 334 Gram Nyayalayas are 
functional in 11 States as on 31.12.2025. 
 

 
13 
1.22 To encourage the States, the Central Government is providing assistance to States for 
Gram Nyayalayas which include ₹ 18.00 lakh per Gram Nyayalaya towards cost of 
establishing the Gram Nyayalaya as a one-time assistance and ₹ 3.20 lakh per Gram 
Nyayalaya per annum as recurring expenditure for a period of three years.  Till date, a sum of 
₹ 93.40 crore has been released under the Scheme of Gram Nyayalayas. The Gram 
Nyayalayas Scheme is now a sub-scheme of the CSS for development of Judicial 
Infrastructure.

1.24 On analysing the Table No 1.8, the Committee observes that out of 488 Gram 
Nyayalayas notified across States and Union Territories, only 334 are functional, indicating a 
significant gap between notification and actual operationalisation . The Committee notes that 

 
14 
while States such as Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Kerala and Uttar Pradesh have made 
relatively better progress in making notified Gram Nyayalayas functional, several States 
including Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh have reported nil 
functional Gram Nyayalayas despite notification and release of funds. The Committee further 
observes  that substantial public funds have been released under the scheme, but the 
outcomes in terms of functionality remain uneven across States, reflecting issues in 
implementation, coordination and monitoring at the State level. Further, the  Department of 
informed the Committee that as per the data uploaded on the Gram Nyayalaya portal, 15,612 
civil and 1,16,518 criminal cases were disposed in the Gram Nyayalayas from January 2025 
to December, 2025. 
1.25 To a reply to the question of the Committee on setting up of Gram Nyayalayas, the 
Department informed that, as on date, no State has submitted a financial proposal for setting 
up a Gram Nyayalaya. Expenditure under the Scheme is contingent upon receipt of proposals 
from the States, either for newly operationalised Gram Nyayalayas or for existing Gram 
Nyayalayas during their first three years of operation. During the current financial year 2025–
26, new Gram Nyayalayas have been set up in the State of Uttar Pradesh, and the financial 
proposal from the State is awaited. Accordingly, the entire provision of ₹2 crore available 
under the Gram Nyayalaya component of the Scheme is expected to be fully utilised during 
the current financial year.   
1.26 The Department in their written submission made stated that it took note of several 
challenges faced in the implementation of the Scheme, including the non-mandatory nature of 
their establishment by States, the functioning of Gram Nyayalayas for only two days a week, 
inadequate infrastructure and ICT support, shortage of judicial officers and supporting staff, 
non-functional Mobile Courts in certain areas, lack of trained Nyayadhikaris, overlapping 
jurisdiction with regular Courts, and limited cooperation from the police and other State 
functionaries. 
1.27 The Committee is of the opinion that Gram Nyayalayas were intended to 
improve access to justice at the grassroots level. By establishing it, it will be able to 
provide speedy, affordable and decentralised justice, especially in rural and remote 
areas. Moreover, the success of Gram Nyayalayas depends on their regular functioning, 
availability of basic infrastructure, presence of trained judicial officers and adequate 
support from the State Governments. 

 
15 
1.28 The Committee observes that since establishment of Gram Nyayalayas is not 
mandatory for States and that, in many States where such Courts exist, they function 
only for two days a week, it restrict the effectiveness in disposal of cases. 
1.29 The  Committee in its 147th Report had recommended  that Gram Nyayalayas 
should function on all working days instead of one or two days a week, the Department 
stated that although the matter falls within the jurisdiction of the State Governments, 
the Department has issued a letter dated 30.04.2025 to the States regarding it. The 
Committee, however, reiterates its recommendation made in 147th Report that Gram 
Nyayalayas must function on all working days in order to effectively reduce the backlog 
of cases at the local level. The Committee believe that early creation of posts and timely 
filling up of vacancies of Nyayadhikaris would ensure uninterrupted functioning of 
Gram Nyayalayas.

Committee, Supreme Court of India primarily for universal computerization of all District 
and Subordinate Court complexes. Initiated in 2010, the Phase-I of the Project concluded at a 
total cost of ₹ 639.14 crore.  
1.31 Phase II of the e-Courts Project was implemented with a total outlay of ₹1,670 crore, 
against which an amount of ₹1,668.43 crore has been utilised. Phase II primarily focused on 
Information and Communication Technology (ICT) enablement of district and subordinate 
Courts during the period 2015–2023. Under this phase, 3,452 Court complexes and 18,735 
Courtrooms were computerised, wide area network (WAN) connectivity was established 
across Courts, and digital case management tools such as the National Judicial Data Grid 
(NJDG) were implemented. 

 
16 
1.32 Phase III of the e-Courts Project, with a total financial outlay of ₹7,210 crore spread 
over four years, was approved by the Cabinet on 13.09.2023. The objective of Phase III is to 
further enhance the use of technology in the judiciary to improve efficiency, transparency, 
and accessibility of justice. Building upon the achievements of Phase II, Phase III aims to 
strengthen digital case management systems, expand virtual Court facilities, and promote the 
use of Artificial Intelligence–based tools for legal research and judicial assistance. 
1.33 Under Phase III, an amount of ₹825 crore was allocated during 2023–24, against 
which an expenditure of ₹768.25 crore was incurred within a period of five months. During 
2024–25, an allocation of ₹1,200 crore was made, out of which an expenditure of ₹1,029.11 
crore was incurred, which is the highest expenditure recorded under the Project so far. For 
2025–26, an amount of ₹1,200 crore was allocated at the RE stage, out of which ₹931.08

₹407.40 crore had been incurred. For the Budget Estimates 2026–27, a total requirement of 
₹1,552.49 crore has been projected for implementation of Phase III of the e-Courts Project, 
out of which an amount of ₹1,200 crore has been provided. The Department submitted the 
achievements of Phase-III of e Courts Mission Mode Project as under:  
  
 The Wide Area Network (WAN) project is aimed at connecting all the District and 
Subordinate Court complexes. So far, 99.5% Court complexes have been connected 
with 10 Mbps to 100 Mbps bandwidth speed. 
 Through the National Judicial Data Grid (NJDG) litigants can access case information 
and more than 34.56 crore orders/judgments. 
 29 Virtual Courts have been set up in 21 States/UTs to try traffic offences. Over 9.54 
crore cases have been handled by these virtual Courts and in more than 90 lakhs 
cases, online fine of more than ₹ 936.59 crore has been realized.  
 Through Video conferencing, District & Subordinate Courts heard 
2,92,04,596 cases while the High Courts heard 97,33,584  cases (totaling 3.89 
crore). Further, VC facilities have been operationalized between 3240 Courts and

 Live streaming of Constitution bench proceedings of Hon’ble Supreme Court of India

1.46 The Department is implementing a Centrally Sponsored Scheme (CSS) for the 
establishment of Fast Track Special Courts (FTSCs) for expeditious disposal of cases relating 
to rape and offences under the Protection of Children from Sexual Offences (POCSO) Act. 
The Scheme was introduced in October, 2019 pursuant to the enactment of the Criminal Law 
(Amendment) Act, 2018 and in compliance with the directions of the Supreme Court of India 
in Suo Motu Writ (Criminal) No. 1 of 2019. The Scheme has been extended on two occasions, 
with the latest extension up to 31.03.2026, at a total outlay of ₹1,952.23 crore, including a 
Central share of ₹1,207.24 crore to be met from the Nirbhaya Fund, for establishment of 790 
Fast Track Special Courts. However, in view of the current allocation of ₹200 crore for FY 
2025–26 and since the proposal for further extension of the Scheme is under consideration, 
an equivalent amount has been proposed under the Budget Estimates (BE) for FY 2026–27. 
1.47 At the inception of the Scheme, allocation of FTSCs was determined on the basis of 
pendency, with the criterion of one FTSC for every 65 to 165 pending cases. Based on this 
criterion, 31 States/Union Territories were initially found eligible to participate in the 
Scheme. However, Arunachal Pradesh opted out citing a very low number of pending cases 
under rape and POCSO categories. The Union Territory of Puducherry joined the Scheme at 
a later stage upon special request and operationalised an exclusive POCSO Court in May, 
2023. The Union Territory of Andaman and Nicobar Islands has conveyed its willingness to 
join the Scheme but has not yet operationalised any FTSC. Further, the State of Jharkhand 
has decided to exit the Scheme vide letter dated 07.07.2025. Consequently, the Scheme is 
presently being implemented in 29 States/UTs. 
1.48 As per data furnished by the High Courts, as on 30.11.2025, a total of 774 FTSCs, 
including 398 exclusive POCSO Courts, are functional across 29 States/UTs. Since inception 

 
22 
of the Scheme, these Courts have disposed of 3,61,055 cases, including 61,431 cases during 
the period January to November, 2025, while 2,44,935 cases remained pending as on 
30.11.2025. The Department is making continuous efforts in coordination with State/UT 
Governments to ensure that all earmarked FTSCs are made operational. 
1.49 Since the inception of the Scheme, the Department has released a total amount of

VACANCIES IN THE DEPARTMENT  
 
1.52 Despite its establishment as an independent Department on 1st January, 2010, it 
continues to be staffed from the common cadre of the Ministry of Home Affairs, with matters 
relating to recruitment and vacancies being handled in coordination with the Department of 
Personnel and Training. 

 
23 
1.53 The Committee notes that against a sanctioned strength of 102 posts, only 63 are 
presently in position in the Department, resulting in vacancies of about 39 per cent, 
which adversely affects its overall functioning. The Committee, in its earlier Reports, 
had expressed concern over the continued dependence of the Department on the 
Ministry of Home Affairs for meeting all its manpower requirements and had 
recommended the establishment of a separate cadre unit for the Department. The 
Committee reiterates the same. 
 
1.53 The Department informed that it has submitted a proposal to the Department of 
Personnel and Training and the Ministry of Home Affairs seeking bifurcation of the common 
cadre and full autonomy in personnel management. A separate proposal has also been sent to 
the Department of Expenditure for allocation of additional manpower to enable independent 
and smooth functioning of the Department. 
1.54 The Department also informed that the Ministry of Home Affairs has conveyed its 
‘No Objection’ for delinking the CSS/CSSS/CSCS cadre from MHA; however, it has 
expressed its inability to spare administrative staff owing to acute shortages across its sub-
cadres and has advised the Department of Justice to pursue the matter further with DoPT. 
Accordingly, the Department has taken up the issue with DoPT and requested expeditious 
consideration. DoPT convened a meeting with MHA and the Department of Justice on 9 
January 2026 and has sought additional information, which is being furnished by the 
Department in consultation with MHA. 
1.55 The Committee is of the view that shortage of staff strength hampers the smooth 
functioning of the Department.  While appreciating the steps taken by the Department 
to bridge this gap, the Committee recommends that the Department should pursue the 
matter of filling up vacancy with DoPT expeditiously and pursue the matter at the 
highest level to ensure early approval and implementation of an independent cadre, 
with clearly defined timelines, so as to address persistent manpower shortages and 
ensure smooth functioning of the Department.

CHAPTER-II 
NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY 
 
2.0 Article 39A of the Constitution of India provides for free legal aid to the poor and 
weaker sections of the society and ensures justice for all. Also, Articles 14 and 22 (1) of the 
Constitution also make it obligatory for the State to ensure equality before law and a legal 
system which promotes justice on the basis of equal opportunity to all. In this background, 
the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was enacted by the Parliament, which came into 
force on 9th November, 1995 to establish a nationwide network for providing free and 
competent legal services to the weaker sections of the society on the basis of equal 
opportunity. 
 
2.1 The NALSA monitors and evaluates implementation of legal aid programmes and 
lays down policies and principles for making legal services available under the Act. In every 
State, a State Legal Services Authority and in every High Court, a High Court Legal Services 
Committee has been constituted. District Legal Services Authorities, Taluk Legal Services 
Committees have been constituted in the Districts and most of the Taluks, respectively, to 
give effect to the policies and directions of the NALSA and to provide free legal services to 
the people and conduct Lok Adalats in the State. Supreme Court Legal Services Committee 
has been constituted to administer and implement the legal services programme insofar as it 
relates to the Supreme Court of India.

SCHEMES/PROGRAMMES OF NALSA 
 
2.5 NALSA is an umbrella organisation mandated to frame policies, allocate grants and 
coordinate and monitor legal services activities of all Legal Services Institutions in the 
country. As per Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, the following 
categories of persons are eligible for free legal services:  
1) All Women and children; 
2) Members of SC/ST; 
3) Industrial workmen; 
4) Victims of mass disaster, violence, flood, drought, earthquake, industrial disaster; 
5) Persons with disabilities; 
6) All Persons whose annual income does not exceed the income limit prescribed by sg 
or high Courts/sub-ordinate Courts and as notified by the State government if the case 
is before the Courts; 
7) Victims of Trafficking in Human beings or beggar; and 
8) Persons in custody. 
 
2.6 The details of activities/programmes regarding Legal Aid and Advice undertaken by 
Legal Services Authorities under the aegis of National Legal Services Authority are as 
follows: 
Legal aid and advice 
2.7  Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 spells out the categories of 
persons entitled to free legal aid. Legal aid and advice primarily comprise of providing Legal 
Aid representation before Courts and tribunals through engagement of panel lawyers in civil 
and criminal cases, Legal Advice and Assistance through Front offices, Legal Assistance at 
pre-arrest, arrest and remand stage and Capacity building programmes for panel lawyers.  
 
2.8 The Legal Services Institutions have about 48,499 advocates on their panels at various 
levels. The persons benefited through Legal Aid & assistance during the financial years 2025-
26 (till December, 2025) is 14, 86,336.  
Legal Services at Pre-Arrest, Arrest and Remand Stage 
2.9  NALSA prepared a protocol in 2019 for providing access to justice to suspects and 
arrestees. The protocol spells out a framework for providing legal assistance at pre-arrest, 
arrest and remand stages. The protocol is expected to fulfill the following objectives: 
 
 To provide legal assistance to needy suspects and arrestees during 
interrogation and other early stages of investigation. 
 To decrease the vulnerabilities of suspects and arrestees. 
 To assist in avoiding unnecessary arrests 
 To assist the arrestees in filing bail applications and furnishing bail bonds.   

 
31 
2.10 Further, the National Legal Services Authority in their written submission informed 
the Committee that, with a view to assisting arrestees in filing bail applications and 
furnishing bail bonds, legal assistance was provided at the district level at the remand stage to 
1,70,912 persons in 2023, 1,83,620 persons in 2024, and 1,90,566 persons during 2025 (up to 
September). For providing legal services at the remand stage, the services of approximately 
6,823 advocates (as on December 2025) have been engaged. 
 
Legal Aid Defense Counsel System (LADCS) 
2.11   The Legal Aid Defense Counsel System (LADCS) was conceptualised in 2019 as a 
systemic reform to strengthen criminal legal aid by establishing a dedicated, professional, and 
accountable defence service at the district level. Following a successful pilot phase and a 
national evaluation, the Scheme was approved as a Central Sector Scheme in March 2024 to 
provide free, competent, and quality legal representation to eligible persons from the earliest 
stage of the criminal justice process. Since its inception, the Scheme has witnessed rapid pan-
India expansion, with LADC Offices being operationalised across a majority of districts, 
supported primarily through assured Central funding to enable institutional stabilisation. 
2.12 For the financial year 2026–27, an allocation of ₹300 crore has been made against a 
projected requirement of ₹558.87 crore. Further, the National Legal Services Authority has 
informed that the Legal Aid Defence Counsel System (LADCS) Scheme will be funded 
entirely by the Central Government up to 2025–26. Thereafter, the Central share will be 
reduced to 75 per cent during the fourth and fifth years (2026–28), 50 per cent during the 
sixth and seventh years (2028–30), and 25 per cent in the eighth year (2030–31). From 2031–
32 onwards, the Scheme will be fully funded by the State Governments. 
2.13 In first phase NALSA implemented LADCS in 365 districts of 22 States/UTs. As on 
December, 2025, the LADCS have become functional in 680 districts. The Committee 
observes that, in comparison to the assigned counsel system, the Legal Aid Defence Counsel 
System (LADCS) demonstrates several operational and institutional strengths, namely: 
 Availability and accessibility of Legal Aid Defence counsel; 
 Effective and efficient representation by seasoned lawyers; 
 Timely and effective Client Consultations; 
 Effective monitoring of legal aided cases; 
 Professional management of legal aid work in criminal matters; 
 Enhanced responsiveness leading to updating of legal aid seekers about the 
progress of their cases.

    Promoting Alternate Dispute Redressal (ADR) Mechanism: 
2.16  Lok Adalats have emerged as a significant pillar of India's justice delivery system, 
offering a speedy, cost-effective, and amicable resolution of disputes. Rooted in the principle 
of conciliation, these alternative dispute resolution forums help prevent prolonged litigation 
and foster harmony between disputing parties. By promoting mutual understanding and 
peaceful settlements, Lok Adalats play a crucial role in reducing the burden on conventional 
Courts.

National Lok Adalats  
2.17  Conceptualized and implemented under the National Legal Services Authority 
(NALSA), National Lok Adalats have been conducted across India since 2015. These 
nationwide sessions facilitate the settlement of cases related to cheque bounce (NI Act), bank 
recovery, labor disputes, service matters, motor accident claims (MACT), compoundable 
criminal offenses, and other civil disputes. 
2.18   In addition to the National Lok Adalat, State Legal Services Authorities and District 
Legal Services Authorities regularly organize State Lok Adalats at the state level to cater to 
the specific needs of local communities, considering regional circumstances and case 
patterns.

COMPENSATION TO VICTIMS OF CRIME  
 
 2.23   Legal Services Authorities play a crucial role in ensuring justice for victims by 
awarding compensation under Section 357A of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), 
in accordance with the Victim Compensation Schemes formulated by State Governments. 
These schemes are designed to provide financial relief and rehabilitation support to victims 
of crime, particularly in cases where the offender is unknown or unable to provide 
compensation. The compensation is granted to help victims recover from the physical, 
emotional, and financial impact of the crime. 
  2.24 With the enactment of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, which 
replaces the Cr.P.C., the provisions related to victim compensation have been further 
reinforced. Under Section 396 of the BNSS, the State remains responsible for compensating 
victims or their dependents through government-funded schemes. This ensures continued 
financial assistance, medical aid, and rehabilitation for victims, strengthening their access to 
justice and welfare. 
2.25 Apart from this, NALSA has also implemented a Compensation Scheme for Women 
Victims/Survivors of Sexual Assault/other Crimes – 2018 which provides financial relief 
and rehabilitation to women victims and survivors of sexual assault and other crimes. To 
address urgent needs, it also provides for an immediate relief and ensures immediate first-
aid and free of cost medical benefits.

MANPOWER REQUIREMENT AT NALSA 
2.34 The Sanctioned posts for NALSA is 45 and as on 31.12.2025 it was functioning with an 
in-position strength of 30 only. The activities of NALSA have increased manifold since its 
inception. It has framed various Schemes to achieve the objectives of the Legal Services 
Authorities Act, 1987. NALSA has been doing various programmes/campaigns for reaching 
out and empowering the weaker sections of society. 
2.35 In their written submission to the Committee, the National Legal Services Authority 
(NALSA) have informed that, pursuant to the Committee’s recommendation contained in its 
143rd Report regarding the creation of 46 new posts, the matter was taken up with the 
Government. Out of the proposed 46 posts, the Government created 11 posts in July 2025, 
while the creation of the remaining 35 posts across various cadres is still awaited. 
2.36 NALSA have further stated that due to acute staff shortage, particularly at the lower 
levels, the Authority has been facing difficulties in effective implementation and monitoring 
of its schemes and programmes, maintenance of data, upkeep of proper accounts, and 
maintenance of other records. 
2.37 The Committee also notes that NALSA have not yet established an internal audit 
Department or cell, and the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG), in its audit 
report, has pointed out deficiencies in the management of records of NALSA. 
2.38 The Committee recommends that the Government expedite the creation of the 
remaining 35 posts sanctioned for the NALSA across various cadres, in a definite and 
time-bound manner, keeping in view the substantial expansion in the functions, 
schemes, and outreach activities entrusted to the Authority.

concrete steps to strengthen its institutional capacity by addressing staff shortages,

of accounts; and efficient record management.

CHAPTER-III 
NATIONAL JUDICIAL ACADEMY, BHOPAL 
 
3.0 The National Judicial Academy (NJA), Bhopal, is an autonomous body established in 
1993 under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. This independent body functions with its 
office at the Supreme Court of India and its campus at Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. This is an 
Apex body which imparts judicial training to Judges/Judicial officers of the country and 
provide facilities for training of ministerial officers working in the Supreme Court, study of 
Court management and administration of justice in the States/Union Territories, organization 
of conferences, seminars, lectures and research in matters relating to Court management and 
administration. The core objectives of the said society have been to foster development of 
National judiciary in the country and strengthen administration of justice, judicial education, 
research and policy formulation. 
 
3.1 The Hon’ble Chief Justice of India (CJI) is the Chairman of the General Body of NJA 
as well as the Chairman of the Governing Council, the Executive Committee and the 
Academic Council of NJA. The affairs of the Academy are managed by a Governing 
Council. The Academy is fully funded by the Government of India. 
 
3.2 The functions of the NJA are to: 
  
 Promote the cause of judicial education; 
 Devise the academic calendar for NJA; 
 Prescribe and approve academic calendars for SJAs; 
 Promote the growth and availability of resources required for judicial training and 
education; 
 Coordinate and monitor the functioning of NJA & SJAs; and 
 Suggest methods for improving judicial education facilities and cooperation among 
NJA and SJAs. NJA and SJAs will submit annual academic calendars of their 
respective academies to the Council for finalization. 
 
3.3 Accordingly, the Annual Academic Calendar for National Judicial Academy is 
finalized every year by the NJA and the academic programs are undertaken by the National 
Judicial Academy as per the finalized Annual Calendar. 
3.4 Further, the National Judicial Academy also organizes the academic programs for the 
foreign judges in line of MoUs executed by the Academy with the foreign authorities on 
behalf of the Ministry of External Affairs, Govt. of India as under: 
 

i. Judicial Service Commission of the Maldives. ii. O/o the Union Chief Justice (OUCJ) under the Supreme Court of Republic of the Union of Myanmar. iii. CHAPTER – IV 
SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
 
4.0 The Supreme Court of India is at the apex of a pyramidal, unified and integrated 
judicial system. Though the political system of the country is federal in nature, the judicial 
system is unitary. The Supreme Court came into existence on 28th January, 1950 and as of 
now it comprises the Chief Justice of India and 33 Judges. The strength of the apex Court was 
enhanced over the years from 8 in 1950 to 11 in 1956, 14 in 1960, 18 in 1977, 26 in 1986, 31 
in 2009 and 34 in 2019, with the increase of case load on it. The Constitution of India 
provides for the Supreme Court to be a Court of record, guardian of liberties & rights and 
also as the final arbiter in most disputes. It is an appellate Court, can review its own 
judgement and in its advisory capacity may answer references by the President on any 
question of law of public importance. The Supreme Court is designated as the custodian of 
fundamental rights and the 'rule of law'. It has power of judicial review and the law declared 
by the Supreme Court is binding on all Courts. 
4.1 The administrative wing of the Supreme Court is called 'Registry'. The Registry is 
divided into two wings - (i) Administrative Wing; and (ii) Judicial Wing. These wings are 
further divided into various Divisions, Branches, Sections and Cells. The Chief Justice of 
India is the Administrative head of the Supreme Court. The highest Administrative Officer of 
the Supreme Court is the Secretary General, the post manned by a judicial officer of the rank 
of a District & Sessions Judge and is of the rank of Secretary to the Government of India. The 
Secretary General is assisted by Registrars, Officers on Special Duty, Additional Registrars, 
Deputy Registrars, officers of other lower ranks and subordinate staff.

Expansion of Supreme Court Building (Project) 
4.6 In their written reply the Supreme Court of India submitted that currently there are a 
total of 17 Court Rooms in the Main Block. The workload of the Supreme Court, along with 
the staff strength, including Hon'ble Judges, has significantly increased over the year 
Consequently, a pressing need for additional space was felt, to accommodate judicial 
functioning, offices, registries, lawyers facilities, waiting areas for litigants, parking facilities 
for vehicles, and other ancillary functions that support the judicial process. 
  
4.7 The Supreme Court also submitted that in order to preserve all judicial operations 
within the current premises of the Supreme Court, the Hon'ble Judges of the building and 
Precinct Supervisory Committee in its meeting on 17.5.2023, under the Chairmanship of the 
then Hon'ble Chief Justice of India, unanimously resolved to approve, in principle, the 
expansion of the Supreme Court building, for development of additional infrastructure to 
cater to both the current and future requirements related to the Supreme Court's judicial 
functioning. Accordingly, the project on ‘Expansion of Supreme Court’ aims to create a 
futuristic judicial infrastructure to provide core facilities for Court hearings with a citizen-
centric approach and for providing state-of-art utilities to the members of the bar, litigants 
and other stakeholders within the existing premises. 
  
4.8 The Project on Expansion of Supreme Court building, a reconstruction of the existing 
premises, was approved on 16th April, 2024 with an outlay of ₹ 795.53 crore to be 
implemented in a period of 60 months (2024-25 to 2029-30) in two phases namely Phase-I 
(34 months) and Phase-II (26 months). The implementing agency is Central Public Works 
Department (CPWD). The work on the project was started on 16.08.2024. Phase I is now in 
its 2nd year of execution. 
   
4.9 The scope of work in phase I involves demolition of two existing buildings, namely 
the Annexe Building (with built up area of 7300 sqm) and Museum Building (built up area of 
1500 sqm). Construction, encompassing a total area of 38258 sqm, is being undertaken. The 

 
51 
total cost involved in Phase I is ₹ 371.99 crore. Once phase I is completed, it will have 14 
number of Court rooms, a Constitutional Court, CJI’s Chamber, 18 Nos Judges chambers, 
lawyers & litigants utilities and two basements for parking for 500 cars.  The structure will 
comprise of two basements, ground floor and five stories above the ground. 
  
4.10 Phase II will commence with the demolition of the East and West Wing of the 
Supreme Court. These wings are connected with semi-circular arc section of the main 
Supreme Court Building, housing Court Nos 6 to 17, with a built-up area of 16340 sqm.  It 
will involve constructions of a total area of 47755 sqm comprising two basements, ground 
floor and four above ground storeys.  The scope of Phase-II construction includes creation of 
14 Court rooms, 24 Judges Chambers, rooms for Registry, Lawyers & Litigants utilities and 
two basements for car parking for 500 cars,  etc. Since the project is a brownfield project, the 
site for Phase II work can be made available only when Phase I is completed and the Court 
rooms are appropriately shifted to the new premises.  
 
4.11 The Committee is of the view that expansion of the Supreme Court of India 
building has become a necessity of the present time, in view of the acute requirement for 
adequate parking facilities; additional chambers for Judges; sufficient space for 
lawyers; security services; and offices for officers of the National Legal Services 
Authority. 
4.12 The Committee recommends that a well-defined and realistic time schedule for 
completion of the expansion project be strictly adhered to by the implementing agency 
so as to ensure timely completion of the project and to avoid any cost escalation or 
requirement of additional funds arising on account of delays. 
4.13 The Committee notes with concern the observations made by the Supreme Court 
of India, pointing to the continued presence of certain officials in the Supreme Court 
Registry for as long as 20 to 30 years. The Committee is of the view that such long 
tenures, if left unregulated, may adversely affect institutional discipline and 
administrative neutrality.  
4.14 The Committee, therefore, emphasises the need for regular review of staffing 
policies, introduction of rotational postings, and strengthening of internal accountability 
mechanisms in court registries to uphold the principles of transparency and efficiency in 
judicial functioning.

VACANCY OF JUDGES IN HIGHER JUDICIARY 
 
15. The Committee notes that as on 31.12.2025, total pendency of cases in the High 
Courts continues to remain at a substantially high level, with 44.67 lakh cases pending 
across 25 High Courts, as per data from the National Judicial Data Grid. Of these, one 
High Court has a pendency exceeding 10 lakh cases, while 16 High Courts have 
pendency of more than 1 lakh cases, reflecting persistent systemic stress on the higher 
judiciary.                                                                                                          (Para 1.60) 
 
16. The Committee observes that the Allahabad High Court accounts for the highest 
pendency, with over 12.07 lakh cases, followed by the Rajasthan High Court (6.88 lakh 
cases) and the Bombay High Court (6.65 lakh cases). Several other High Courts, 
including Madras, Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka, Punjab and Haryana, also record 
pendency well above the national average, indicating region-specific capacity and 
caseload challenges.               ( Para 1.61) 
17. The Committee notes that civil cases account for the bulk of pendency in most 
High Courts, while criminal case pendency has also been rising. To address this issue 
Alternate Dispute Redressal (ADR) may be promoted  and these case may diverted to 
Arbitration, Mediation, Conciliations and Lok Adalats. Making pre-litigation 
Mediation mandatory in Civil disputes also helps in reducing pendency. 
(Para 1.62) 
18. The Committee is of the view that incremental improvements in disposal alone 
are not sufficient to address the problem of pendency. Urgent measures such as timely 
filling up of judicial vacancies, strengthening of infrastructure, better case management, 
and increased use of technology and alternative dispute resolution mechanisms are 
required.                                   (Para 1.63)

with the High Courts and State Governments, prepare Courts-specific, time-bound 
action plans to reduce pendency and filling of vacant post immediately. The Committee 
also recommends phased expansion of live-streaming of Court proceedings to all 
Courts, including High Courts and Subordinate Courts, and suggest exploring the use 
of AI-based tools to support judicial work and improve efficiency.                (Para 1.64)

Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to submit the Report 
on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred Sixty Third Report on Demands for Grants 2026-
27 pertaining to the Legislative Department (Ministry of Law and Justice). 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India projected under various Demands 
for Grants for the upcoming financial year need to be voted by Parliament. As a sequel thereto, 
Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred to concerned 
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close scrutiny thereof under Rule 
270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. While making scrutiny 
of Demands for Grants, the Committee has made an appraisal of performance, programmes, 
policies of the Legislative Department vis-à-vis expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of 
India in the current Financial Year.

and the Election Commission of India, for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by the 
Committee.

the Secretary, Legislative Department (Ministry of Law and Justice), Sr. Deputy Election 
Commissioner, Election Commission of India (ECI) along with senior Officers of the Department 
and ECI in its sittings held on the 19th February, 2026.

the following:-

1.9 Legislative Department does not have any statutory or autonomous body under its control.  
It has two other wings under it, namely, the Official Languages Wing (OLW) and Vidhi Sahitya

(i) Official Languages Wing is a successor organisation of the Official Languages 
(Legislative) Commission under the Legislative Department and is responsible for 
preparing and publishing standard legal terminology and for translation into Hindi of 
all the Bills to be introduced in Parliament, as well as all Central Acts, Ordinances, 
and subordinate legislation as required under the Official Languages Act, 1963. The 
Official Languages Wing is also responsible for arranging translation of the Central 
Acts, Ordinances, etc., into the Official Languages specified in the Eighth Schedule 
to the Constitution as required under the Authoritative Texts (Central Laws) Act, 
1973. The Official Languages Wing also provides grants-in-aid to various registered 
voluntary organisations engaged in the promotion and propagation of Hindi and 
other regional languages and to organisations directly engaged in the publication of 
legal literature and the propagation of Hindi and other languages in the field of law. 
Functions of Official Languages Wing:- 
a) Preparation of authoritative texts in Hindi of all legislations prepared by the 
Legislative Department; 
b) Preparation of Hindi texts of all statutory Notifications under Section 3(3) of 
the Official Languages Act, 1963;  
c) Work relating to the Coordination Committee of Hindi Speaking States for 
ensuring effective coordination among committees such as the Hindi 
Salahkar Samiti and the Official Languages Implementation Committee for 
the evolution of uniform legal phraseology and model standard clauses in 
Hindi and their publication thereof; 
d) Publication of diglot editions of Central Acts and their regional language

Hindi. These publications are widely sought after in the Hindi-speaking States. The 
three publications, namely, Uchchatam Niyayalai Niranai Patrika, Uchcha Niyayalai 
Civil Niranai Patrika and Uchcha Niyayalai Dandik Niranai Patrika have been in 
publication since 1968, 1978 and 1979, respectively.  This Wing is also responsible 
for sale of official diglot edition of Central Acts, Constitution of India, Election 
Manual, Legal Glossary etc. 
Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan Functions:- 
a) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan (VSP) aims to provide Hindi text of the judgments 
in English passed by Hon’ble Supreme Court of India and various High 
Courts; 
b) Publication of High standard text books in Hindi on various subjects in the 
field of law; 
c)  To award various prizes for the best publications in Hindi in the field of law; 
d)  Sale of Hindi publications of the Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan and diglot editions 
Central acts, Constitution of India, Legal Glossary, Hindi Law Text Books 
and Election Manual; and 
e)  Promotion and propagation of Hindi in the legal field by holding 
conferences, training programmes, seminars and book exhibitions all over 
India  
(iii) Vidhi Sahitya Prakashan publishes three Law Journals in Hindi: 
a. Uchchtam Nyayalaya Nirnaya Patrika (since 1968) ; 
b. Uchcha Nyayalay Civil Nirnaya Patrika (since 1978); and 
c. Uchcha Nyayalay Dandik Nirnaya Patrika (since 1979). 
1.10 The organisational set-up of the Legislative Department includes officers at the level of 
Secretary, Additional Secretary, Joint Secretary and Legislative Counsel, Additional Legislative 
Counsel, Deputy Legislative Counsel and Assistant Legislative Counsel, along with other support 

7  
staff. Work relating to legislative drafting in the case of principal legislation and the scrutiny and 
vetting of subordinate legislation has been distributed among various Groups. Each Group is headed 
by a Joint Secretary and Legislative Counsel or an Additional Secretary, as the case may be, who in 
turn are assisted by a number of Legislative Counsels at different levels. The Secretary of the 
Legislative Department acts as the Chief Parliamentary Counsel and the Additional Secretary is in 
charge of all subordinate legislation. 
 
1.11 Legislation is one of the major instruments of articulating the policy of the Government. In 
this context, the Legislative Department plays an important role to secure the policy objectives 
which the Government may wish to achieve through legislation. 
(i) Legislative Department not only performs functions as the primary Department for 
drafting the legislation initiated by the administrative Ministries and Departments but 
also initiates legislative proposals in respect of the matters with which it is 
administratively concerned. 
(ii) Legislative Department drafts the Finance Bill to give effect to the financial proposals 
of the Central Government every year.  This exercise is undertaken in the Legislative 
Department on the budget proposals being brought before it by the Ministry of 
Finance.   
(iii) For the purpose of convenience, the various subjects on which Bills are drafted in the 
Legislative Department at the behest of administrative Ministries/ Departments can be 
broadly categorised as under: - 
(a) Constitutional amendments; 
(b) Economic and corporate laws; 
(c) Civil Procedure and other social welfare legislation; 
(d) Criminal laws; 
(e) Repeal of obsolete laws; and 
(f) Miscellaneous laws. 
1.12 Institute of Legislative Drafting and Research (ILDR) was established in the Legislative 
Department, Ministry of Law and Justice in January, 1989 and it is an ISO 9001:2005 certified 
institute, to scale up the capabilities and availability of trained Legislative Counsel to deal with 
legislative proposals and to impart theoretical, clinical, practical knowledge as well as off-campus 
training in Legislative Drafting and Research to officers of Central Government Departments, State 
Government/Union Territories, Public Institutions and Government Bodies. 

8  
ELECTION COMMISSION OF INDIA 
1.13 The Legislative Department is the administrative Department for the Election Commission 
of India, an autonomous constitutional authority. Election Commission of India (ECI), since its 
establishment in 1950, has been instrumental in ensuring free, fair and transparent elections in 
India. Articles 324 to 329 of the Constitution of India define the functions, responsibilities, structure 
and powers of the ECI. These Articles mandate the Commission to conduct elections to the Lower 
and Upper Houses of Parliament and State Legislative Assemblies and to the high offices of the 
President and Vice-President of India at regular intervals. 
(i) As per Article 324 of the Constitution of India, “The superintendence, direction and 
control of the preparation of the electoral rolls for, and the conduct of, all elections to 
Parliament and to the Legislature of every State and of elections to the offices of 
President and Vice-President held under this Constitution shall be vested in a 
Commission (referred to in this Constitution as the Election Commission)”.  
(ii) Election Commission currently consists of Chief Election Commissioner and two 
Election Commissioners. 
(iii) The President appoints Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners. 
They have tenure of six years, or up to the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.  
 
1.14 The salary and other conditions of service of the Chief Election Commissioner of India and 
other Election Commissioners are governed by the “Chief Election Commissioner and Other 
Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023”. 
According to this Act, the salary, allowances and other conditions of service of the Chief Election 
Commissioner and other Election Commissioners shall be the same as those admissible to a Judge 
of the Supreme Court. The Commission has a separate Secretariat at New Delhi. Different divisions 
in the Commission are headed by Deputy Election Commissioners and Director Generals, who are 
officers of the rank of Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary to the Government of India. They are 
generally appointed on deputation with the Commission. 
1.15 The functions of the Election Commission under the Constitution, the Representation of the 
People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) and this Act, or under the rules made thereunder may, subject to such 
general or special directions, if any, as may be given by the Election Commission in this behalf, be 
performed also by a Deputy Election Commissioner or by the Secretary to the Election 
Commission—Section 19A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. 
 

9  
1.16 It registers political parties and allots symbols to them and ensures inner party democracy in 
their functioning by insisting organizational elections at periodic intervals. Political parties 
registered with the Commission are granted recognition at the State and National levels on the basis 
of their poll performance at general elections according to criteria specified by it. It implements 
Model Code of Conduct (MCC) for smooth conduct of free and fair elections. It also observes 25th 
January as National Voters' Day to encourage young electors to take part in election process.  
1.17 The electoral expenses on account of conduct of elections to the House of the People and the 
State Legislative Assembly are borne by the Central Government and the concerned State 
Government, and in case of simultaneous elections, the expenditure is to be shared on 50:50 basis 
between Central and the concerned State Government. The initial expenditure is borne by the 
respective State Governments, and on submission of the audited report, the Central Government’s 
share is reimbursed through the Legislative Department.  
1.18 The Election Commission has its independent Secretariat for the work relating to the smooth 
conduct of elections to Parliament and State Legislatures, and there is an exclusive demand 
(Demand No. 66), i.e. voted expenditure under which budgetary allocation is sought for running the 
activities of Election Commission of India. 
1.19 The Commission has purchased land from DDA at Sector-9, Dwarka, New Delhi for 
construction of additional office building for Election Commission. The budget earmarked by the 
Ministry of Finance under Capital Section includes nominal provision for carrying out pre-
construction activities for additional office building of ECI. Since, during next financial year 
nominal funds (₹1 lakh) have been earmarked.  Proposal for additional funds would be moved to 
the Ministry of Finance at appropriate time as soon as detailed construction plan is received from 
NBCC.

Repealing of Obsolete and Redundant Laws  
2.29 The Department in its written submission has stated that 1725 obsolete and redundant laws 
have been repealed by Government of India through various Repealing and Amending Acts, 
Finance and Taxation laws since 2014. This has reduced compliance burden on citizens and ensured 
ease of doing business and ease of living for citizens.  The Parliament had enacted the Repealing 
and Amending Act, 2025 (37 of 2025) to repeal certain enactments and to amend certain other 
enactments. Vide Second Schedule of the said Act, it has amended the Code of Civil Procedure, 
1908 (5 of 1908) and the General Clauses Act, 1897 (10 of 1897); and omitted section 213 of the 
Indian Succession Act, 1925 (39 of 1925) and consequential amendments are, inter alia, made in 
section 3 and 370 of the Act. 
2.30 The amendments in the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 and the General Clauses Act, 1897 
are made to meet the challenges faced in the light of the merger of Registered Post services with 
Speed Post.  The amendments in the Indian Succession Act, 1925 removed the discriminatory 
linkage of mandatory probate on the basis of religion of the testator and depending on geographical 
location of the property. The amendment in the Indian Succession Act, 1925 will reduce 
unnecessary court intervention, promotes uniform and fair applicability of succession laws across 
the country and is a major step towards ease of living.   Thus, by omitting section 213 of the Indian 
Succession Act, 1925 in its entirety, the Government has transformed probate from a mandatory 
requirement into an optional measure. 
2.31 The Committee appreciates the steps taken so far in this regard and desires that the 
Department may make further efforts to repeal obsolete and redundant laws through a 
regular and time-bound review mechanism and evolve a systematic framework for periodic 
identification of outdated statutory provisions in consultation with stakeholders. The

Parliament in strengthening legislative outputs through deliberation and value addition. 
2.34 The Committee is of considered view that the increasing volume and complexity of 
legislative work necessitates continuous strengthening of institutional capacity. The 
Committee desires that the Legislative Department undertake a comprehensive assessment of 
its workload, staffing pattern and skill requirements, particularly during peak legislative 
periods, and evolve structured internal review and quality control mechanisms. The

Composition and Staff Strength

Commission of India and appointment of Chief Election Commissioner and other Election

3.8  The Committee observes from the information furnished by the Election Commission of 
India that a significant number of posts remain vacant against the sanctioned strength. Out of the 
145 sanctioned Group ‘A’ posts, 36 posts are vacant. Similarly, against the total sanctioned strength 
of 313 posts in Group ‘B’ (Gazetted and Non-Gazetted), 48 posts remain vacant. Further, out of the 
373 sanctioned posts in Group ‘C’, as many as 167 posts are vacant. The Committee also notes that 
13 posts out of 16 sanctioned posts of Canteen Staff are vacant. Overall, 264 posts remain vacant 
out of the total sanctioned strength of 847 posts, indicating a vacancy level of about 31%.  
3.9 The Committee is of the view that such persistent vacancies may adversely affect 
administrative efficiency and service delivery. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the Commission should expedite the recruitment process in a time-bound manner to fill up 
the vacant posts and ensure optimal utilization of human resources so that the functioning of 
the Commission is not hampered due to manpower shortages. 
3.10 The Committee notes the decision of the Election Commission of India, as conveyed vide 
Press Note dated 24.06.2025, to undertake a Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls in 
the State of Bihar, aimed at ensuring inclusion of eligible electors, deletion of ineligible names and 
enhancing transparency in the electoral process. The Committee takes note of the proposed house-

25  
to-house verification by Booth Level Officers and the uploading of relevant documents on ECINET 
with restricted access, as well as the involvement of political parties through Booth Level Agents. 
3.11 The Committee is of the view that the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of Electoral Rolls 
should be carried out in a fair, transparent and inclusive manner, ensuring that no genuine elector is 
excluded and that electors are not subjected to undue hardship during the revision process. The 
Committee emphasises the need for adequate safeguards for vulnerable sections, including senior 
citizens, persons with disabilities, economically weaker sections and migrant populations.  
3.12 The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Election Commission of India should 
put in place robust monitoring mechanisms at all levels to ensure uniform implementation of 
the revision process, while also ensuring strict adherence to data privacy and security 
protocols in respect of documents uploaded on the Election Commission Integrated Network 
(ECINET). These measures, in the view of the Committee, would help enhance transparency 
and strengthen public confidence in the integrity of the electoral rolls.  
3.13 The Committee observes that voters in remote, rural, tribal and hilly areas face significant 
practical difficulties in accessing polling stations, with electors in certain cases required to travel 
long distances, sometimes up to 10–15 kilometres. The Committee further notes that strict 
application of population-based norms for the location of polling stations in such difficult and 
sparsely populated areas may result in avoidable hardship to voters and could adversely impact 
voter participation, besides posing operational challenges for the election machinery. 
3.14 The Committee recommends that the Election Commission of India may adopt a 
flexible and area-specific approach in the location and rationalisation of polling stations in 
remote, rural, tribal and hilly regions, while broadly adhering to the prescribed norms. The 
Commission may consider relaxing the norms in genuinely difficult terrains, taking into 
account geographical constraints, connectivity and voter convenience. The Committee further 
recommends that periodic accessibility assessments may be undertaken to identify hardship-
prone areas so that no elector is effectively deprived of the opportunity to vote due to distance 
or terrain-related barriers. 
3.15 The Committee observes that concerns were raised regarding certain practical challenges 
faced by voters at polling stations. These include difficulties in reading the details displayed on 
Electronic Voting Machines due to inadequate lighting and enclosure-related darkness, uneven 
visual prominence of election symbols on EVMs, gaps in voter slip distribution leading to 

26  
confusion and disputes at polling booths. The Committee also notes the need for greater 
transparency and accuracy in dissemination of voter turnout data to avoid ambiguity and confusion. 
 
3.16 The Committee recommends that the Election Commission of India may examine the 
feasibility of introducing suitable technical and procedural measures to enhance voter 
convenience, including improved lighting or backlit display for EVMs, ensuring visual parity 
among election symbols, strengthening and verifying voter slip distribution mechanisms, and 
rationalising the establishment of polling stations so that no village is left without reasonable 
access to a polling booth. The Committee further recommends that the Commission may put 
in place a transparent and real-time system for dissemination of voter turnout data, with a 
view to minimising disputes and enhancing public confidence in the electoral process. 
3.17 The Committee, during deliberations, discussed certain systemic and operational aspects of 
the electoral process relating to the Election Commission of India, including the continued reliance 
on indelible ink despite increasing digitisation, transparency in the manufacture of Electronic 
Voting Machines (EVMs) and Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trails (VVPATs), difficulties faced by 
migrant workers in exercising their franchise. The Committee note that these issues, if not 
adequately addressed, may affect voter confidence and inclusiveness in the electoral process. 
3.18 The Committee, recommends that the Election Commission of India may consider 
adopting appropriate technological measures to strengthen the principle of “one person, one 
vote,” enhance transparency in the functioning of EVMs and VVPATs, facilitate the 
participation of migrant workers in the electoral process, and improve polling station 
infrastructure, so as to enhance voter confidence and accessibility.

INTRODUCTION 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on 
Personnel, Public Grievances, Law and Justice, having been authorized by the Committee to 
submit the Report on its behalf, do hereby present this One Hundred Sixty Fourth Report on 
Demands for Grants 2026-27 pertaining to the Department of Legal Affairs. 
2. In accordance with the constitutional requirement under Article 113, the estimated 
expenditure of Ministries/Departments of Government of India projected under various 
Demands for Grants for the upcoming financial year need to be voted by Parliament. As a 
sequel thereto, Demands for Grants of the relevant Ministries/Departments stand referred to 
concerned Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee to make a close scrutiny 
thereof under Rule 270 of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of 
States. While making scrutiny of Demands for Grants, the Committee has made an appraisal of 
performance, programmes, and policies of the Department of Legal Affairs vis-à-vis 
expenditure made out of Consolidated Fund of India in the current Financial Year. 
 
3. In the Report, scrutiny of Demand No. 65 pertaining to the Department of Legal Affairs 
for the Financial Year 2026-27 has been made by the Committee. 
 
4. During the course of examination of the above Demands, the Committee heard the 
views of the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs, Representatives of Income Tax Appellate 
Tribunal; Director, Indian Law Institute; Joint Secretary & Law Officer, Law Commission of 
India,; Registrar, India International Arbitration in its sitting held on 19th February, 2026.  
 
5. The Committee, while making its observations/recommendations, has mainly relied 
upon the following: 
(i) Presentations made by the Secretary, Department of Legal Affairs; 
(ii) Presentations made by the representatives of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal 
and Indian Law Institute;  
(iii) Detailed Demands for Grants of the Department for the Financial Year 2026-27;  
(iv) Detailed Explanatory Notes on the Demands for Grants 2026-27  received from 
the Department;  
(v) Annual Report of the Ministry for the Year 2025-26 and the latest available 
Annual Reports of the attached Offices/Institutions/Organisations of the 
Department;

Committee Secretariat; 
(vii) Written clarifications to the points/issues raised by Members in the meeting of
