CHAPTER–V
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
CENTRAL VIGILANCE COMMISSION
49.0 The Central Vigilance Commission (CVC) was established in 1964, as an apex body for
exercising general superintendence and control over vigilance administration, through the
Government of India Resolution of 11.2.1964. The main mandate of the Commission was based
on the report of the Committee on Prevention of Corruption, popularly known as the Santhanam
Committee. The establishment of the Commission was considered essential for evolving and
applying common standards in deciding cases involving lack of probity and integrity in
administration.
49.1 The Resolution empowered the CVC to undertake inquiry into any transaction in which a
public servant is suspected or alleged to have acted for an improper purpose or in a corrupt
manner irrespective of his or her status. Through subsequent ordinances and legislations, the
Government has added to the functions and powers of the Commission. Subsequent to the
directions of Hon’ble Supreme Court in the judgement in the Writ Petition filed in public interest,
by Shri Vineet Narain and others in Jain Hawala Case, the Government promulgated an Ordinance
in 1998. The Ordinance of 1998 conferred statutory status to the CVC and the powers to exercise
superintendence over functioning of the Delhi Special Police Establishment, and also to review the
progress of the investigations perta ining to alleged offences under the Prevention of Corruption Act,
1988 conducted by them.
49.2 In 1998, the Government introduced the CVC Bill in the Lok Sabha in order to replace the
Ordinance, though it was not successful. The Bill was re-introduced in 1999 and remained with
the Parliament till September 2003, when it became an Act after being duly passed in both the
Houses of Parliament and with the President’s assent. The provisions of the Act include inquiries
into offences alleged to have been committed by certain categories of public servants of the Central
Government; corporations established by or under any Central Act; Government Companies;
Societies; and local authorities owned or controlled by the Central Government; and for matters
connected therewith or incidental thereto. To give effect to the provisions of the Act of 2003, the
Commission exercises all powers and functions entrusted to it under the Government of India
Resolution No.24/7/64-AVD dated 11.2.1964, which are not inconsistent with the provisions of the
Act. To effectively implement the provisions of the CVC Act, the Commission continues to
discharge its functions under the CVC Resolution 1964.
49.3 Many years have passed since the enactment of CVC Act of 2003, and prevention of
corruption continues to be the prime concern of the country. In response to a Public Interest
Litigation which was filed in the Supreme Court on account of the murder of Satyendra Dubey,
the Supreme Court directed the Government to designate a suitable machinery to act on complaints
from “whistle blowers” till such time as a suitable legislation was enacted to that effect. The
Central Government while implementing the directive of the Supreme Court, has reposed its faith
on the CVC. Through a Resolution dated 21 st April, 2004 the Government has designated the
Central Vigilance Commission as the agency to act on complaints from “whistleb lowers” till such
time as the Parliament passes a law on the subject. According to the Government Resolution on
“Public Interest Disclosure and Protection of Informer”, 2004 the Commission has been entrusted
with the additional responsibility of keeping the identity of the complainant secret and the power
32

33
to take action against complainants making motivated or vexatious complaints. There is no
restriction on jurisdiction of the Commission in the said Resolution.
49.4 The Central Vigilance Commission is assisted by a Secretary, two Additional Secretaries and
other staff which include nine officers, an Officer on Special Duty and four Under Secretaries. In
addition, there are fourteen Commissioners for Departmental Inquiries who are nominated to
conduct departmental inquiries relating to major penalty proceedings on behalf of the disciplinary
authorities in serious and important disciplinary cases.
49.5 In principle, the jurisdiction of the Commission extends to all organizations to which the
executive power of the Union extends. Section 8(1)(d) of CVC Act restricts its jurisdiction with
respect to level of employees for inquiry into complaints to Group A level officers and such level
of officers as may be notified by the Central Government. The Commission however retains its
residuary powers to call for any individual case in respect of employees other than those who are
within its normal advisory jurisdiction. In addition, cases of difference of opinion between the CBI
and the concerned administrative authorities, in respect of employees who are not within the normal
jurisdiction of the Commission, are also resolved by the Commission.
49.6 The advisory role of the Commission extends to all matters on vigilance administration
referred to it by the organizations/departments. However, it is mandatory on the part of the
Departments to seek its advice on reports called for by the Commission. The investigation reports
furnished by the CVO or by the CBI are examined in the Commission and, depending upon the
circumstances and facts of each case, the Commission advises (a) initiation of criminal and/or
departmental proceedings against the concerned public servant(s); (b) or issuance of administrative
warning to him/her; (c) or the closure of the case. The Commission’s advice at this stage is termed
as first stage advice. The departmental proceedings could be for imposition of a major or a minor
penalty. In those cases where major penalty proceedings were advised, on conclusion of the inquiry
proceedings, the Commission’s second stage advice is required to be sought along with the inquiry
report and other inquiry record. The Commission has to be consulted where inquiry proceedings
could not be conducted due to special circumstances. While no second stage advice is required to
be obtained in minor penalty cases, where the administrative authorities propose exoneration on
consideration of defence statement, the Commission is required to be consulted.
49.7 Each Department/organization, to which the advisory jurisdiction of the Commission
extends, has a vigilance unit headed by a Chief Vigilance Officer(CVO). The CVOs act as the
extended arms of the Commission and for all practical purposes represent the Commission in
respect of vigilance matters, particularly with reference to junior officers, who fall outside the
jurisdiction of the Commission. They are required to provide experts’ assistance in advising the
head of the concerned organization in all vigilance matters concerning it. The CVOs serve as the
vital link between the Departments/organizations and the CVC and it is their function to advise the
organizations to establish effective systems and procedures and periodically monitor their
compliance to minimize factors, which provide opportunities for malpractices. On the punitive side,
the CVOs are required to ensure speedy processing of vigilance and disciplinary cases.
49.8 According to the Annual Report of the CVC, as the Designated Authority, the Commission
has laid down a procedure for lodging complaints under the above Resolution. This has been given
wide publicity and has also been put on the Commission’s website. Only such complainants
submitting the complaints as per this procedure would be entitled to protection.
50.0 Some areas of concern highlighted in the Annual Report of CVC
(i) The Central Vigilance Commission, even after its statutory status, continues to be a purely
advisory body. The superintendence of vigilance administration by CVC is severely curtailed by the

34
proviso to Section 8(1)(h) of the CVC Act whereby such superintendence is sought to be
constrained by the directions related to vigilance matters issued by the Government and by
adherence to policy matters decided by the Government. The Commission’s experience over the
years is that if the credibility of vigilance administration has to rise, such administration has to be
independent of Government. Similarly, in many areas, it is the policy and loopholes therein which
give rise to corruption, and if the Commission cannot take the initiative and be proactive, vigilance
administration will have to be less than optimally effective.
(ii) Apart from this, the Commission has also realized the need to undertake some inquires
directly, where there is apprehension on the part of the complainant that entrusting it to the
organizational vigilance may not yield proper and quick result. The Commission has, on the basis
of a scientific study of work in the organization, proposed strengthening of the resources of the
Commission. This has to be addressed most urgently.
(iii) The Commission’s role is advisory when it comes to recommending disciplinary action
against the officers coming within the purview of the Commission under Section 8(2) of the CVC
Act. Again, such recommendations are purely advisory, when it comes to punishment at the
conclusion of the Departmental disciplinary proceedings. The service rules excepting in the case of
banks, do not provide even for consultation with the Commission at both stages. These are
currently governed by executive instructions and convention. It is necessary that the first stage
advice, namely advice of the Commission on the basis of the facts brought out before it on the
nature of proceedings to be initiated against the delinquent public servant, has to be made
mandatory and binding on the disciplinary authority. This will also eliminate the inordinate delay
noticed in initiating action against the public servants on the basis of complaints and investigation
thereon. At the second stage, on conclusion of inquiry proceedings in the case of certain categories
of Government servants coming under the purview of UPSC, the Commission has also pointed to
the desirability of eliminating dual consultation. This issue has not yet been resolved by the
Government. The Commission would reiterate its suggestion that such consultation can be
dispensed with, excepting perhaps where the CVC’s recommendations is for stiff major penalty,
namely, compulsory retirement, removal from service or dismissal. This will eliminate delays and
enable the Commission to discharge its obligations under the Act more effectively and meet the
expectations of the complainants.
(iv) A detailed procedure has been laid down within the Commission for processing the
complaints. The Commission’s experience has been that  the bulk of complaints related to
grievances. The Commission had, in its earlier report, also observed that creation of an
Ombudsman, atlcast in major Government Departments having significant public dealing, could
address this important area of public concern, so that institutions like the Central Vigilance
Commission are not approached by the common citizens for redressal of their grievances.
(v) The Commission has no investigation wing of its own. Therefore, it depends entirely on the
Chief Vigilance Officers of respective organizations for the investigation into complaints and fixing
responsibilities on the errant public servants and to follow up appropriate departmental action
against them. As emphasized by the Commission time and again, the vigilance administration in
Government rests on the CVOs in the various departments/organizations.
(vi) The Commission has strongly spelt out the need for a full time CVO in major departments,
particularly, those having a number of important PSUs under their administrative control. In other
departments, there could be a system of one full time CVO for a group of departments as is the
case with Financial Advisors.
(vii) In Departments like Railways, Telecom, CPWD, Post and Telegraph, CBDT and CBEC, the
Commission has strongly recommended for an “outsider” to be posted as the CVO.

35
(viii) To ensure the independence and neutrality of the CVO, the Commission has recommended
that the CVOs’ tenure could be approved for five years subject to the Commission certifying the
satisfactory performance/functioning of the CVO after three years, so that there is an automatic
extension in such cases for a further period of two years without leaving any discretion to the
CEOs of the organizations or the Ministry concerned.
(ix) It is immensely important that the post of CVO is not allowed to remain vacant.
50.1 The Secretary, CVC deposed before the Committee as follows:
“...Sir, there is no doubt that our Commission is an advisory Commission and our first stage
advice and our second stage advice are all advisory and not mandatory. And, it is happening
in quite a few cases, as a result of which, our annual report is becoming thicker and
thicker every year. When we give our advice, it is upon the disciplinary authority to accept
it or not to accept it. Increasingly, it is seeming as if they are not accepting the CVC’s
advice. It only enters into the Annual Report as a paragraph and is placed on the Table of
the House. That is what happens. So, the question is, can we make the Commission to have
a little more teeth?...”.
50.2 The CVC, in its written reply to the Committee, has stated as follows:
“The Commission has also observed that many a time the Disciplinary Authority does not
adhere to the Commission’s first stage advice in vigilance cases and decides in deviation to
the Commission’s first stage advice. It has also been noted that there is a tendency to dilute
the disciplinary proceedings by poorly drafted charge sheet or lack of focus on the
allegation leading to poor success rate in the major penalty proceedings resulting in minor
penalty or even exoneration. The Commission has been making efforts and asking
organizations to send draft charge sheet, details of evidence etc. even at the time of sending
papers to the Commission for seeking Commission’s first stage advice. But the compliance
is very poor.
Therefore, the Commission would like its First Stage advice in vigilance cases to be made
mandatory to be implemented by all Government of India organizations, Public Sector
Undertakings and Banks”.
50.3 In the reply furnished by CVC, it has been stated thus:—
“After the establishment of CVC, which is the apex body for consultation in matters relating
to disciplinary action against the officers of All India Services and Group ‘A’ Officers, the
provision regarding consultation with UPSC also, not only leads to duality of authority but
also is a cause for inordinate delays in finalizing the disciplinary proceedings leading many
a times to the superannuation of the charge sheeted official before a penalty can be
imposed. Some times there is a conflict of views between CVC and UPSC about the penalty
to be imposed due to difference in perception between the two agencies. The Commission
being an expert agency on vigilance cases and having been made paramount in matters
pertaining to vigilance administration, it is only appropriate that it should have the final word
on disciplinary matters. Such overlapping of authority creates unnecessary delay and
hindrances in the finalization of cases, besides undermining the Commission’s authority and
which would be counter productive”.
50.4 The Committee, in its 14th Report, had recommended that the recommendations of the CVC
regarding better vigilance mechanism should be implemented without further delay.
50.5 In the ATR furnished by the Ministry, it has been stated:

36
“The proposal of CVC to appoint full time and outsiders CVOs in Ministries/Departments
of Government of India is under examination. The comments of important Ministries/
Departments have been received and a note for consideration of the Committee of
Secretaries is being submitted”.
50.6 The Committee strongly recommends that the concerns raised by CVC should be
addressed immediately to ensure independence, impartiality and credibility of the Apex anti-
corruption body. An instruction may be issued to all offices of Government of India that
before issuing charge sheet, at least in major penalty cases, the consultation with CVC
should be mandatory. It is of the considered view that the issue of overlapping of authority
with the UPSC and appointment of full time CVOs require urgent consideration and action.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that amendment in the corresponding provisions
pertaining to the UPSC may be made so that UPSC may deal with the recruitment matters
only and CVC with vigilance matters.
51.0 In the Annual Report of CVC, it has been stated that the average time taken by the
Commission in tendering its advice is about four weeks; more than 77 per cent of its advices are
tendered within three weeks of receipt of the cases.
51.1 The Committee is pleased to note that in majority of the cases, the CVC tenders
advice promptly.
52.0 As per the Annual Report of CVC, it has adopted Bureau of Indian Standards 15400 in its
complaints handling process.
52.1 The Committee appreciates this initiative of the Commission and hopes that this will
ensure proper and expeditious processing of complaints.
53.0 According to the Annual Report of CVC, it interacted with NGOs such as the Centre for
Media Studies, Citizens’ Forum Against Corruption and Transparency International Limited to gain
useful inputs about the public perception of corruption and the possible countermeasures needed.
53.1 The Committee applauds this proactive initiative of CVC.

limit, as the case may be.  Limitation as to the income does not apply in the case of persons belonging to weaker sections,
such as, the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes, women, children, handicapped, etc.  The annual income limit fixed by the 
Central Government for cases before the S upreme Court is Rs.50, 000/- at present.  At the fourth Annual Meet of the State 
Legal Services Authorities held under the aegis of the NALSA on 29 th February 2004 and 1`st March 2004 at Kolkata, i t 
was resolved to raise the income ceiling in terms of section 12(h) of the said Act, from Rs.25, 000/- to Rs.50, 000/- pe r 
annum in respect of cases before High Courts and Courts subordinate thereto.  Goa, Gujarat, U.T. of Chandigarh and Delhi 
have since raised the income ceiling to Rs.50, 000/-.  While the income limit has been raised , the number of beneficiaries
has increased.

LOK ADALATS 
  
32.       Lok Adalat is one of the Alternative Dispute Resolution, mechanisms.  The institution of Lok Adalats has been 
given a statutory status by the Legal Services Authorities Act,  1987.  The statutory support to Lok Adalats has helped in 
taking justice to the door-steps of the poor and needy and made justice quicker and less expensive.  The award of a Lo k 
Adalat is deemed to be the decree of a Civil Court, is final and binding on all parties and no a ppeal lies before any cour t
against it.  
  
33.       With a view to providing compulsory pre-litigative  mechanism for conciliation and settlement of disputes relating
to public utility services, the Parliament  amended the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.  The amended Act stipulates 
establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats for exercising jurisdicti on in respect of disputes relating to public utility services,
such as, transport service, postal, communication, supply of power, service in hospital/dispensary, insurance service, etc. 
  
34.       Subsequent to the coming in to force of the said Amendment Act, the States of Haryana, Jharkhand, Rajasthan an d
U.T. of Chandigarh have established Perm anent Lok Adalats.  Steps are being take n to establish such Lok Adalats in the 
remaining States/U.Ts. Several State Lega l Services Authorities have informed that Permanent Lok Adalats could not be
established for want of funds and infrastructure.

LEGISLATIVE DEPARTMENT 
  
54.       Legislative Department is one of the oldest Departments, which was set up in the pre-independence period in 1883, 
and at one time it was part of the Department of Home. The ma in task of the Legislative De partment is to draft Bills fo r
enactment of new laws or amendment of the existing laws, and to advise and assist th e Administrative Ministries an d
Departments in legislative matters at all the stages, and also  to process the Bills at all stages, till President’s assent is 
received and the Act is published in the Official Gazette. 
  
55.       Apart from preparing the Bills in the light of th e legislative proposals, the Department finalises the Statements o f
Objects and Reasons, Financial Memoranda , the Notes on Clauses, in connection with introduction of Bills, and the
Memorandum regarding Delegated Legislation, where ever required. 
  
56.       The Department mainly performs the following functions:- 
             
(i)                  It handles the legislative business of the Government of India; 
(ii)                Administratively handles election laws; 
(iii)               Administers more than seventy Acts relating to subjects in Concurrent List such as the Registration
Act, the Contract Act, Transfer of Property Act, marriage and divor ce, civil procedure, arbitrations,
etc.; 
(iv)              It translates into Hindi all the Central Bills, Acts  and Constitution of Indi a and into other official
languages contained in the VIII Schedule of the Constitution; and 
(v)                It brings out reports in Hindi the decisions of the Supreme Court of India and various High Courts.  
It also awards prizes for various books in law brought out in Hindi.

•                    Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union territory or exclusion of a Union territory from the
jurisdiction of a High Court. 
  
78.       It is the Nodal Department in so far as the adminis tration of judicial services in States is concerned, although the
actual responsibility of judicial administration below the High Court level rests with the concerned State Governments and

of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs since long.  That Committee, from time to
time, in its reports, has made important observations and recommendations relating to implementation of the scheme.  That 
Committee, in its 86 th report on Demands for Grants (2002-03) of the Mini stry of Law and Justic e had, made important 
recommendations which are summarised below: 
  
While Centrally Sponsored Scheme relating to Infrastructural Facilities for the Judiciary had been a good beginning
in the direction of smooth administra tion of justice, the funds provided unde r this scheme not seem to be enough,
particularly looking at the demand projected by the States vis-à-vis funds earmarked by the Planning Commission.  
There is a strong case for increasi ng the budget allocation for the Judiciar y.  The Government should conside r 
enhancing the central support to the State Governments.  The Government  should also redesign the pattern o f 
Centre-State share, so that the States would have less budgetary pressure on them.   
  
The Committee endorses the observations made by the Committee on Home Affairs in its earlier Reports on
Demands for Grants of Ministry of Law and Justice and recommends that the G overnment should be liberal in providing
grants to State Governments for development of infrastruc tural facilities for the judiciary, and persuade the State
Governments for efficient utilization of the grants for the purpose.

89.       The Eleventh Finance Commission had sanctioned setting up of 1734 fast tr ack courts, for expeditious trial of long
pending sessions cases and also cases involvi ng under trials, who remain in  jails for a period of more  than two years.  As 
on 23rd July, 2004, 1488 courts had become functional.   They have disposed of 4,83,958 ca ses, out of 10,29,792 cases 
transferred to them.  The fast track courts were star ted on the basis of the recommendation by the XIth Finance 
Commission for the period 2000-05.  The De partment of Justice has already taken up with the XIIth Finance Commission
to continue the Fast Track Courts beyond 2005 also.   The ove rall functioning of the Fast Tr ack Courts is the primary
responsibility of the respective State Governments and the conc erned High Courts.  The cases are transferred to Fast Track 
Courts under the directions of the respective High Courts.  
  
90.       An amount of Rs.413 crore ha s been released so far directly to the St ates/UTs by the Ministry of Finance.  The

91.       Fast Track Courts are taki ng up sessions cases pending for two years or more and the cases of under-trials in jails 
on priority.  The Scheme is expected to  effect substantial saving in expenditure on jails besides addressing serious human
rights problems.  Disposal of sessions and other cases, pending for a long time, will have a salutary effect on law and order
and crime situation.  The fast track courts are doing an excellent job in quick disposal of long pending cases and their work
have been appreciated by the Supreme Court of India.  Supreme Court is monitoring the setting of Fast Track Courts by the
States.  The Central Government has also  been requesting all the State Government s to set up Fast Track Courts at the
earliest.

Court and High Courts, by bringing in, if nece ssary, a suitable legislation.  The Minist ry had stated that in tune with the 
then Government’s commitment to the setting up of a Nati onal Judicial Commission, a Constitution Amendment Bill was
introduced on 9th May, 2003 in the Lok Sabha, which proposes to am end articles 124,217,224 and 231 of the Constitution,
relating to appointment of Judges in th e Supreme Court and the Chief Justices of the High Courts and appointment an d
transfer of Judges of the High Courts, and for inserting a new Chapter IV-A in part V of the Constitution for setting up of a 
National Judicial Commission. 
  
108.     The Constitution (Ninety-Eighth Amendment) Bill, 2003,  introduced in the Thirteenth Lok Sabha, was referred to
the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs for examination and report.  Before the 
Committee could complete its work, the Th irteenth Lok Sabha was dissolved cons equent upon which the Bill lapsed.  The 
Committee was informed that at present there is no proposal for introduction of any Bill fo r setting up of the National
Judicial Commission. 
  
109.     During the course of Committee’s deliberations with  the representatives of the Ministry, a point was made fo r
adequate representation of SCs, STs and OBCs in the higher judiciary to meet the ends of social justice and equity. 
  
110.     The Committee reiterates its earlier recommendation to restore the pre  - 1993 position in the matter of appointment 
of Judges of Supreme Court and the Chief Justices of High Courts and appointment and transfer of Judges of High Courts. 
  
BENCHES OF SUPREME COURT  
  
111.     The Committee has been recommending time and ag ain for setting up of Benches of Supreme Court in far-flung 
areas, with a view to providing justice to the poor, for whom it  is impossible to visit the Na tional Capital.  The Ministry 
had, during the consideration of the Dema nds for Grant (2002-03), stated that the Chief Justice of India conveyed that the 
issue relating to setting up of Benches of  Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-Eastern parts of the country, as 
recommended by the Committee, was considered in the Full Court on 30 April, 2001, and the latter had unanimously found
no justification in deviating from their earlier. Resolution on the subject, which had further said that the said demand,
could not be accepted.   
  
112.     The Committee strongly felt that establishment of Benches of Supreme Court in Southern, Western and North-
Eastern parts of the country would facilitate the litigants to avail justice from the apex court, without traveling to Delhi
from far away places.  During consideration of Demands fo r Grants (2003-04) the Committe e had asked the Government 
Page 22 of 252nd report of Law and Justice
7/17/2008http://10.21.217.2/book2/reports/personnel/2ndreport.htm

to approach the Chief Justice of India for review by the Supreme Court of its earlier decision.   
  
113.     Government had informed the Committee that Arti cle 130 of the Constitution provides that “the Supreme Cour t 
shall sit in Delhi or in such other place or places as the Chief Justice of India may, with the approval of the President, from
time to time appoint.”  The recommendation of the Committee, as contained in its 101 st Report was again referred to the 
Chief Justice of India on 17 th April, 2003 to reconsider the same.  The re sponse in this regard was still waited.  The 
Minister for Law and Justice has requested the Chief Justice to send his reconsidered views in the matter.  
  
114.     The Committee recommends that the Government should decide its course of action to resolve the matte r
expeditiously. 
  
PENDENCY OF CASES 
  
115.     As per the latest information available as on 1 st July, 2004,  29,315 cases were pe nding in the Supreme Court; 
35,27,282 in different High Courts and 2,27,57,693 cases were pending in the Subordinate Judiciary. 
  
116.     The Government has taken the following steps to clear the pendency:- 
  
•                    The Government has been constantly reviewing the ac cumulation of arrears in C ourts.  Besides increasing 
the Judge strength from time to time, various steps have been taken by the Courts, viz; grouping of cases 
involving common questions of law, constitution of specialized benches and organizing Lok Adalats a t
regular intervals, etc. 
•                    The Government has also encouraged alternative m odes of disposal including mediation, negotiation and
arbitration.  Special tribunals lik e Central Administrative Tribunal, St ate Administrative Tribunals, Income
Tax Appellate Tribunals, Family Courts, Labour Courts, Consumer Courts  etc. have been set up to expedite
disposal of cases.  Information te chnology is being used in generation of cause lists, providing information
to the litigants/Advocates etc. for speedy disposal of cases. 
•                    Fast Track Courts (FTC) fo r the disposal of long pending cases,  particularly sessions cases and cases
involving undertrials in jails are being set up. 
•                    Central Government has sa nctioned a grant of Rs.502.90 crore, based on the recommendations of the
Eleventh Finance Commission, for the creation of 1734 Fast Track Courts in the Country. 
  
117.     The Committee on Home Affairs, in its 101 st Report on Demands for Grants  (2003-04) had urged upon the 
Government to consider fresh initiatives to arrest pendency of cases in va rious courts.  Government had initiated some 
measures to arrest and clear such pendency.  It had also requested the State Governments/High Courts to earmark a portion
of the Fast Track Courts to dispose of senior citizen’s cases, on priority basis. 
  
118.     About the impact of such measures the Departme nt of Justice had informed the Committee that the process o f
judicial reforms is a continuous one, and therefore, it would not be possible to assess the impact of such measures to reduce
pendency of cases.  However, the Department has been focusing on computer ization of the entire subordinate judiciary,
which will impact on the arrears of cases.   
  
119.     The Committee hopes that the Government, with its resolve as contained in the National Common Minimum
Programme, would be able to drastically cut the delays in the High Courts and the Lower Judiciary. 
  
DEMAND NO.64   SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
  
120.     Demand No.64 in the detailed Demands of  Grants of the Ministry pertains to  the Supreme Court of India.  The 
expenditure to be incurred on the Suprem e Court of India is ‘Charged’.  The to tal Budget Estimates of the Supreme Court 
of India for the year 2004-05, under the Re venue are Rs.34.68 crore as against Rs.39.51 crore in Revised Estimates for the
year 2003-04.   
  
GENERAL  
  
121.     The Committee notes that in almost all Ministries a separa te head for medical expenses has been created, excepting
the Ministry of Law and Justice.  The Committee feels that if  other Ministries could open this head, this Ministry coul d
also have taken timely action, to ensure uniformity in the system.

DELIMITATION COMMISSION
6.1. On a specific query raised about the progress of delimitation work, the Ministry submitted
the following written reply:—
“The Delimitation Commission was constituted in July, 2002. It became functional in
November/December 2002. The Commission - in terms of the Constitutional provision–
was to delimit the constituencies on the basis of 1991 census figures. By June 2003
the Commission had completed almost 60% of its work. The totality of the
Commission’s work (all the Parliamentary constituencies and the Assembly
constituencies in all the States in the country) would have been completed by
November/December, 2003. But it could not be done because the Parliament amended
the Constitution by the Constitution (Eighty-Seventh Amendment) Act, 2003, which
provides that the delimitation work shall be done by the Commission on the basis of
the 2001 census and not the 1991 census figures. As a consequence, the work done
by the Commission on the basis of the 1991 census became non-est by the operation
of law. The Commission, however, started preliminary work on the basis of the
provisional 2001 census figures, which were available. But the preliminary work could
not be taken to the logical extent because; even the provisional 2001 census figures
regarding the Schedule Castes and Schedule Tribes were not available.
The 2001 Census figures for most of the States were published on
31st December, 2003. Thereafter the Commission took-up the work of collecting data
and tabulating the same. While the process was going on, the Lok Sabha was dissolved
and fresh elections were declared. The Commission has five Lok Sabha Members from
each State as its associate members. Where the number of MPs in a State is less than
five, all of them become Commission’s members. With the dissolution of the Lok
Sabha, the associate members ceased to be members by operation of law. Even
otherwise during the elections, the fieldwork by the Commission was almost stopped.
After the constitution of the Fourteenth Lok Sabha, the Commission requested Hon’ble
Speaker to nominate associate members to the Delimitation Commission from each
State. After receipt of the nominations, the Commission restarted the delimitation work,
which is progressing on a tight schedule.

4
The delimitation of the Lok Sabha and Assembly constituencies in all the States is a
time consuming work. Under the scheme of the Act associate members are to be
associated with the delimitation work from the very beginning. As a consequence there
have to be more than one meeting with the associate members from each State.
Thereafter, the draft delimitation proposals are published in newspapers and suggestions
and views are invited from the public. Finally, the public meetings are held by the
Commission in all the States and the draft finalized, after that.”

Accountant Member) from the SC/STs and rest of the proposed vacancies would be filled up
as and when the Recruitment Rules are finalized as per the directions of the Appointments

9
created with zeal and enthusiasm, are still non-functional. The Committee is perturbed over

NATIONAL LEGAL SERVICES AUTHORITY (NALSA)
7.5 Budgetary allocation (2007-08) for NALSA has been made as Rs. 17.50 crore.
7.6 National Legal Services Authority (NALSA) has been constituted under section 3 of the
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 in the year 1995 to provide free and competent legal services
to the weaker sections of the society with the objective to ensure that opportunities for securing
justice are not denied to any citizen for the reason of economic or other disabilities. To be eligible
for seeking legal aid under the NALSA, the annual income limit fixed by the Central Government
for the cases before the Supreme Court is Rs. 50,000 at present. Out of twenty eight States Legal
Services Authorities, and 7 Union Territories, Andhra Pradesh, Arunachal Pradesh, Bihar,
Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh,
Mizoram, Orissa, Punjab, Sikkim, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, West Bengal, U.T. of
Chandigarh, Delhi have raised the income ceiling limit to Rs. 50,000 per annum to provide free legal
aid under Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry,
during the period from the 1st April, 2006 to the 30th September 2006, more than 1.90 lakh
persons have been benefited through legal aid services. Out of them, 13,191 persons belonged to
the Scheduled Castes, 8,383 to the Scheduled Tribes, 23,964 were women and 962 were children.
7.7 The Committee appreciates that its recommendation (15th Report on the Demand for
Grants (2006-07), that more and more States and UTs should raise the income-ceiling limit
for providing free legal aid under NALSA’s Scheme has re sulted in 19 States and
3 UTs raising the limit to the prescribed level of Rs. 50,000 per annum. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry should speed up the entire process so that the
income-ceiling limit throughout the Country remains uniform and larger number of persons
can get benefit under the scheme.
7.8 The Committee in its 15th Report on the Demands for Grants 2006-07 had recommended
that “the counsels engaged for the poor under the legal aid programme are paid meagerly; and as
a result thereof good and reputed lawyers do not come forward to take up the cases. Even Senior
Advocates do not take up such cases. As a result the poor litigants feel that legal aid being provided
to them is mere eyewash. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the fee structure for the
legal aid counsel should be reasonably enhanced so that the experienced and competent lawyers are
attracted and motivated to take up/accept the cases of the legal aid beneficiaries with full
enthusiasm Moreover, the fee structure should be made uniform throughout the country”. The
Ministry replied as under:—
“The issue of raising of fee structure of Legal Aid Counsel and having a uniform
structure throughout the country was discussed in the All India Meet of the State Legal
Services Authorities at Kochi, Kerala. It was felt that fee structure should be such as

10
to attract the talented, competent and committed lawyers. Now, a Committee
comprising three senior Judges has been constituted to consider the matter and submit
its report within 3 months. On receipt of the Committee’s report action will follow.”
7.9 The Committee feels appreciates that its recommendation for raising of fee structure
of Legal Aid Counsel has resulted in constitution of a Government Committee to look into
the matter. The Committee desires that the Department may apprise it as and when any
decision is taken into the matter.

7.12 The Committee in its 15th Report had recommended that NALSA should submit/prepare a
consolidated scheme, covering all its scheme and programme for formulating a centrally sponsored
scheme with component to provide hundred per cent funding by the Union Government for
operationalising NALSA plans. In response there to the Ministry has replied that with regard to
providing 100% funding by it for operationalising NALSA’s plans under Centrally Sponsored
Scheme, the Central Government is releasing grants to the National Legal Services Authority, i.e.,
the Central Authority (Section 14 of the Act). The Central Authority can also receive any grants,
donations made to it by any other person and also any amounts under the orders of any court
[sub-section (1) of section 15 of the Act]. the Central Authority makes grants to the State Legal
Services Authorities for meeting the costs of legal services provided under the act [sub-section (2)

11
of section 15]. Further, the State Leal Services Authorities are constituted by the concerned State
Governments [Sub-section (1) of section 6]. The administrative expenses of the State Authority
shall also be defrayed out of the Consolidated Fund of the State [sub-section (7) of section 6].
In view, of this there is no scope for evolving any Centrally Sponsored Scheme with 100% funding
to the State Legal Services Authorities for covering their infrastructural requirements.
7.13 The Committee notes that NALSA has launched a laudable mission for legal
empowerment of all the sections of the society, yet, certain grey areas need to be addressed
by the Ministry. Moreover, non-utilisation of grants by the States Legal Services Authorities
is another area of concern. The Ministry should effectively monitor not only utilisation of
the funds but also implementation of the schemes and programmes of NALSA. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the constraints of funds should not come in the
way of successful implementation of the scheme. The Ministry should, therefore, allocate
additional funds to help operationalise the various programmes to be undertaken by NALSA
at RE stage. The Committee also feels that the actual benefit of this scheme is not gaining
access to the poor litigants and the programmes are confined to high profile areas or capital
cities only and publications in English papers. The Committee therefore recommends that
the NALSA should organise legal awareness programmes all over the country at village and
slums in general and in North Eastern region in particular. The Committee has been
apprised by the Ministry that there is no scope for evolving any Centrally Sponsored
Scheme with component to provide hundred per cent funding by the Centre for
operationalising NALSA’s plans since under the provisions of the Legal Services Authorities
Act 1987 the Central Government is releasing grants to NALSA (Section 14 of the Act). The
Committee feels that the vision with which the various programmes will be launched by
NALSA could be achieved only by way of proper planning. The reason behind stressing cent
percent funding by way of Centrally Sponsored Scheme is that the programmes launched
can be easily monitored, targets set can be achieved, and the financial crunch should not
be a problem. Moreover there will be a vision to achieve set targets in a time bound
manner. The Committee, therefore, recommends that if required, necessary changes in the
Legal Services Authorities Act 1987 may be made for incorporating the idea of evolving any
Centrally sponsored Scheme with component to provide cent percent funding by the Centre
for operationalising NALSA’s plans.
7.14 Lok Adalat is an important constituent of NALSA. Permanent Lok Adalats under section 19
of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 have been established in almost all the States. However,
Permanent Lok Adalats for Public Utility Services under section 22B of the Legal Services
Authorities Amendment Act, 2002 have been established in States viz. Assam, Andhra Pradesh,
Arunachal Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka, Kerala, Meghalaya, Tripura, Bihar, Haryana, Jharkhand,
Punjab, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Andaman and Nicobar and U.T. of Chandigarh. The State Governments
of Uttrakhand and Government of N.C.T. of Delhi have also approved the proposal for
establishment of Lok Adalats. So far as Jammu and Kashmir is concerned, amendment to the Act
is required. During the period from 1st April, 2006 to 30th September, 2006, 28,844 Lok Adalats
were organized. These Lok Adalats settled 11,00,000 cases. The State Authorities, where the
Permanent Lok Adalats have not been established, have been directed by Hon’ble Executive
Chairman to pursue the matter with their respective State Government to provide infrastructure and
requisite funds for establishment of Permanent Lok Adalats U/S 22B of the Act. However, the State
Governments’ response as reported by the State Authority is not encouraging.
7.15. The Committee notes that only thirteen States and two Union Territories have
established so far the Permanent Lok Adalats for public utility services and such proposals
have been cleared so far by Uttarakhand and National Capital Territory of Delhi. The
remaining States/Union Territories are still in the process of consideration of the proposal

12
whereas for Jammu and Kashmir an amendment in the Act would be required. The
Committee expresses its concern over the slow pace of establishment of Permanent Lok
Adalats for public utility services. It also notes that after amendment of the Legal Services
Authorities Act in 2002 the establishment of only a few such Permanent Lok Adalats
manifests a lackadaisical approach. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier
recommendation (15th Report Para 7.13) that the Ministry should make all out efforts in
the direction of establishing Permanent Lok Adalats in the remaining States and UTs. It
would be appropriate if the Ministry chalks out a time-bound programme in consultation
with the State Legal Services Authorities for establishing these Lok Adalats and monitor the
pace of implementations thereof and also encourage the State Government to be more
forthcoming in their response.
7.15A The Committee further recommends that a formal study be made to ascertain the
quantum of funds required for establishing permanent Lok Adalats by the various State
Authorities. This apart, the Committee desires that other problems faced by the
Department in establishing Permanent Lok Adalats may also be brought before it so that
the Committee is enabled to recommend ways and means to remove hurdles and
bottlenecks coming in the way of establishing Permanent Lok Adalats.
LAW COMMISSION OF INDIA
7.16 The Committee finds that the 17th Law Commission was constituted on 1st September, 2003
for a period of three years and came to an end on 31st August, 2006 with Hon’ble Mr. Justice M.
Jagannadha Rao as its Chairman. Shri. R.L. Meena, as its Vice-Chairman. The 18th Law Commission
has been reconstituted with effect from September 1, 2006 for a period of three years ending
August 31, 2009. The Chairman and Members are yet to be appointed.
7.17 The Committee has been appraised that the Law Commission has since submitted 196
reports out of which 52 are still pending. The Seventeenth Law Commission has presented ten
Reports (186th to 195th reports) so far out of which four reports (192nd, 193rd, 194th and 195th)
are under examination.
7.18 The Committee feels that vacancy should be filled up immediately on the retirement
of the Chairman/Member and there should not be a gap even for a day to ensure continuity
of the Commission’s work. The Committee notes that the Ministry has started laying of the
statement of pending Law Commission’s Reports once in a year before the Parliament. The
Committee further hopes that the Ministry would be pursuing the Administrative
Departments/Ministries for implementation of the Reports of Law Commission.
7.19 The Committee feels that the Law Commission’s reports form the basis for review
of the judicial system and framing, amending and repealing the legislations as per the needs
of the changing circumstances. Thus, the role of the Commission assumes special
significance in the Indian judicial and legislative system. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that the reports of the Commission should be implemented in letter and spirit
and the Ministry should make concerted efforts to ensure timely implementation of the
recommendations contained therein. The Committee therefore, reiterates its earlier
recommendation (15th Report Para 7.16) that the Ministry should consider providing
statutory backing to the Law Commission on the pattern of the other countries like U.K.
and Canada, etc., so that it could function more effectively with the desired empowerment.

7.38 The Committee is unhappy to note that ICADR which is going to be one of the
premier institutes in the field of Arbitration and Conciliation and whose building was
constructed from the Grants given by the Government, has leased its building to the Sixth
Pay Commission, Department of Legal Affairs and National Tax Tribunal. The Committee is
anguished that the building constructed from the Grants of the Government could be leased
out to other Governmental bodies. The Committee therefore, strongly recommends that
ICADR must not earn money by leasing out its building to Governmental bodies. On the
contrary, it should make all efforts in attracting foreign arbitration cases and in turn be
the hub of arbitration centres. The Committee also recommends that Ministry should look
into the issue and provide a status report in this regard while submitting the Action Taken
Reply. Further, ICADR should be in a position to give financial and strategical support to
develop new Centers by Private Participation such as Palkivala Center of Arbitration in
Chennai. Moreover, the Committee recommends that the Government Departments and
Public Sector Undertakings should include a clause in the agreements entered into with
other parties, which provides for referring matters to ICADR for arbitration in the event
of dispute, instead of going to the courts directly. This should be made mandatory by issuing
appropriate directions to all the Departments of Government of India, Public Sector
Undertakings, Public Sector Enterprises etc. The Committee has already recommended in its
9th Report on the Arbitration and Conciliation (Amendment) Bill, 2004 that sole arbitrators
who are working as Government Officers discharging dual role should be gradually
eliminated and that the ICADR or such other Private Arbitration Centers should be allowed
to be involved in it for effective Alternative Dispute Resolution.

FREE ELECTORAL ROLLS

ELECTRONIC VOTING MACHINES (EVMs)
7.47 The Election Commission of India had purchased the Electronic V oting Machines for the
first time in the year 1989-90 and started their use on experimental basis in November, 1998

22
onwards only. While referring to the successful experimental use of Electronic voting Machines in
the then held Parliamentary and Assembly Elections in many constituencies/States on selective basis,
the Election Commission sought to use these machines on regular basis in elections and requested
the Government for making available adequate number of these machines so as to over all polling
stations in the country. The Election Commission is of the view that once a constituency has voted
with EVMs; it would not be practical or desirable to go back to the traditional ballot boxes for poll
in such constituencies in future. It would, therefore, be necessary to start planning to provide
the full requirement of EVMs, on a permanent basis, to each State in a phased manner. An amount
of Rs. 150 crores during the year 2000-2001, Rs. 200.61 crores during the year 2002-2003,
Rs. 303 crores during the year 2003-2004 and Rs. 130 crores during the year 2004-2005 were
accordingly provided to the Election Commission for purchasing the machines from two Public
Sector Undertakings, namely, the Electronics Corporation of India Limited, Hyderabad and the
Bharat Electronics Limited, Bangalore on 50:50 basis. All stakeholders, namely, the political parties,
the electorates and the staff involved in election duty have accepted the machines. Also, the use
of the machines in its present form and with existing technology has passed the test of judicial
scrutiny, whenever it has been challenged. The General Election, 2004 to the Lok Sabha and
elections to the Legislative Assemblies of States/Union territories were conducted using the
electronic voting machine. These Machines are also successfully used for conducting elections to
the local bodies in various States and Union territories.
The Election Commission has been taking up the rationalization of polling stations from time
to time and on the basis of feed backs received from States; it felt the need for reducing the voter
strength per polling station in order to ensure voter convenience and an orderly poll within the
stipulated polling hours. This has resulted in the increase of polling stations across the country and
consequential requirement of about 2.5 lakh V oting Machines to cope up with the additional
requirement. The existing EVMs, which are being used presently, was introduced in the year 1990
after technical evaluation by Expert Committee headed by Professor P. V . Indiresan. On the basis
of experience in using Electronic V oting Machines and inputs gathered from the States and taking
into account the technological advancements that could be incorporated in the Electronic V oting
Machines to be purchased in future, the Election Commission initiated a process of consultation
with the manufactures of Electronic V oting Machines  i.e.  Bharat Electronics Limited and Electronic
Corporation of India. Based on that, the manufactures have come out with a new version of
Electronic V oting Machines without changing basic design and concept of the Electronic V oting
Machines, incorporating certain features that would result in better management of elections. The
new features/improvement incorporated in the new version of the Electronic V oting Machines are-
(a) Real time Clock (b) Time Stamping of every event conduct on the machines (c) Battery Power
indication (d) Provision for power saving mode (e) Display of Hourly Total (f) Facility for totalizing
the results from various control units and (g) Switch over from numeric to alpha-numeric display.
During the current financial year, an amount of Rs. 225 crore has been provided to the Election
Commission for purchase of the upgraded version of approx. 2.5 Lakh Electronic V oting Machines.
The Committee was also apprised that EVMs were used in the recently concluded Assembly
elections in the States of Manipur, Uttarakhand and Punjab. Out of a total of 37,000 EVMs used,
complaints in 344 nos of EVMs were received. In most of the cases, it was found to be human
errors like improper linking of the balloting unit with control unit, improper fitting of Battery, etc.
The decision as to whether EVMs would be used in the elections to the local bodies of the
States are taken by the State Election Commissions. After taking a decision in this regard, the State
Election Commission requests the Election commission of India for providing EVMs to them on
loan basis. The Election commission of India, in turn, approaches the Ministry of Law and Justice
to obtain the consent of the Ministry before loaning the EVMs to the State Election Commissions.
This Ministry has so far, on different occasions, has given approval for loaning of EVMs on certain

23
terms and conditions on test basis to the State Election Commission of States of Kerala, Andhra
Pradesh, Tripura, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Haryana, NCT of Delhi, Bihar and Union Territories
of Andaman and Nicobar Islands and Daman and Diu.
7.48 The Committee feels that being one of the largest democracies of the world, the
Ministry’s constant endeavor should be directed to ensure that elections are held in free
and fair manner. Necessary infrastructure, of which, EVMs constitute a major part, should,
therefore, be in place at the time of holding elections. The Committee is satisfied that its
recommendation for upgradation of old EVMs and the process of procurement of 2.5 lakhs
new upgraded EVMs has been implemented. The Committee recommends that the
Committee constituted to decide the technical worthiness of the 1989-90 model EVMs may
be asked to submit its Report by the stipulated date of 25th May, 2007 so that the said
Report becomes useful in assisting the Committee likely to be constituted for disposing off
the old EVMs. The Committee hopes that the old EVMs would be discarded and new
upgraded EVMs would be used in all the coming elections and help to get the election
results early and in a speedy manner.
ELECTORS PHOTO IDENTITY CARDS (EPIC)
7.49 The Committee has been informed that the use of electors’ photo identity cards by the
Election Commission is slowly and surely making the electoral process simple, smoother and
quicker. A decision was taken by the Election Commission of India in 1993 to issue photo identity
cards to electors throughout the country to check bogus voting and impersonation of electors at
elections. The electoral roll is the basis for issue of EPICs to the registered electors. The electoral
rolls are revised every year with 1st January of the year as the qualifying date. All persons who
attain 18 years or above as on that date are eligible for inclusion in the electoral roll and can apply
for the same. Once they are registered in the roll, they would be eligible for getting an EPIC. The
scheme of issuing the EPICs is, therefore, a continuous and ongoing process for the completion
of which no time limit can be fixed as the registration of electors is a continuous and ongoing
process (excepting for a brief period between the last date for filing nomination and completion
process) on account of more number of persons becoming eligible for the right of franchise on
attaining the age of 18, current programme will always constitute a residual part of the
programme. The Election Commission’s (EC) continuous effort is to provide the EPICs to the
electors who are left out in the previous campaigns as well as the new electors. The Election
Commission, which is overall in charge of implementation of the scheme of issuance of photo
identity cards to electors and has been monitoring its progress on regular basis, has informed that
more than 48.98 crore electors representing 70.39% of the eligible voters in the country have been
provided photo identity cards.
As on date, approximately 30% electors are yet to be issued voter identity card. It has been
the endeavour of the Commission to achieve 100% coverage under the EPIC scheme, as far as
practicable, in a time bound manner. Even though efforts have been constantly made to cover all
the electors under the EPIC scheme, various reasons such as natural calamities, engagement of
administrative machinery, which also attends to other works than election work, apathy of voters
themselves are some of the reasons why progress has been uneven. While in some States/UTs such
as Kerala, Punjab, West Bengal, Lakshadweep and Puducherry the EPIC card percentage is above
90%, the EPIC programme has not actually taken place due to various reasons in Assam and
Manipur.
The Commission is concerned about the fact that said 30% gap in issuance of EPIC is
continuing despite annual EPIC campaigns being undertaken. Factors that contribute to this gap are
(1) persons who attain eligibility for the first time are registered every year. This may be about

24
2%, (2) Due to death but not deleted about 1% and (3) intercity and intra city migration in major
metropolitan towns which may account to 7% to 8%. It has also come to the notice of the
Commission that migrating electors in most cases do not mention their EPIC number, if any, issued
at the place of their previous residence in the application form field for inclusion of name at their
new place of residence. Therefore, though the name is included in the part of the roll where the
elector shifts, the EPIC number remains blank and this adds numbers to the non-EPIC holder
statistics. At the place of origin, till such time, such persons’ names continue and it adds numbers
to EPIC-holders statistics creating a false picture.
Another phenomenon noticed is that from the backward and poor areas of the country
(Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh, Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, etc.) a lot of seasonal migration of the unskilled
persons takes place (mainly of men but some women too) and semi-permanent migration takes
place of skilled persons (mainly of men) but their names are not deleted from the voters list at
the place of origin as the family members who reside there, want their names to continue for
emotional and more mundane (to prevent property disputes etc.) reasons. As such persons are not
available for photography, EPICs cannot be issued and the gap remains uncovered for long as EPIC
campaign period may not coincide with the period of their visits to their homes. These are major
areas of concern. This scene gets complicated further in urban areas where other photograph-based
identity documents (like Passports, Driving Licenses, Departmental or Employer-given IDs) are
available and urbanites do not show any enthusiasm for obtaining EPICs as it involves spending
their precious time to go to a Photo location for a document which anyway has relevance for them
once in 5 years only and for which they already have alternatives.
The Commission has instructed that the EPIC number once issued will be valid throughout
the Elector’s life even if address changes. If the EPIC is declared to be an acceptable identity
Document for all Governmental purposes, the Electors will see a value to it beyond the once-in-
5-years poll day usage. With plans of Election Commission to have all States Elector database being
made available all over India, searching for an EPIC number can be made easy and if combined
with Photo of the Elector in the database, tracking would become easy. Therefore one of the ways
in which this problem is being addressed is to prepare electoral rolls with the photograph of
electors.
The Commission has decided to modify the statutory application Forms 6, 8 and 8A to
allow optional submission of photograph by the elector at the time of fresh inclusion, correction
or transposition of entry within the constituency.
Pending modification of the Forms, in West Bengal and Haryana, the facility of submitting
photograph as an option has been experimented through non-statutory forms prescribed by the
Commission. The photo is used for generating EPIC and also printing the image in the photoroll.
7.50 Issue of Photo Identity Cards to voters is one of the constituents of the budget of the
Legislative Department. Budget Estimates (Non-Plan) for the year 2006-07 under this heading was
Rupees 42.24 crores as compared to Rupees 22.24 crores during the current financial year
(2007-08).
7.51 The Committee notes that as on the 1st January, 2006, total electors in the country
were 695,750,887 and the number of the electors, who have been issued Photo Identity
Cards, is 489,758,562 which constitute 70.39%, of the total voters. Thus, there remains a
shortfall of nearly 30% of those who are yet to be covered under the EPIC scheme. The
Committee also notes that the Election Commission has started a campaign for this purpose
by identifying some States for a pilot project. The Committee feels that the Commission has
not achieved the desired goals despite the fact that considerable time has elapsed since the
inception of the EPIC scheme. It has also come to notice of the Committee that in Madhya

25
Pradesh, the Photo Identity Cards issued to the concerned person bears the photograph of
animals like tiger and dogs instead of having the photograph of bonafide citizens. The
Committee feels such type of action is unwarranted and tells a lot about the tall claims

SIMPLIFICATION OF LEGISLATIVE LANGUAGE
7.56 The Committee in its 15th Report on Demand for Grants had recommended that efforts
should be made by the Department in the direction of simplifying the language used in law. In
response thereto the Department has replied that:—
“Official Languages Wing has clarified that terms and expressions used in Hindi version
of Central Laws were decided and approved by the various experts of the then official
Languages (Legislative) Commission. This Commission consisted of legal and language
experts of all India repute and finalized translation of most of the major Acts. We can
not deviate much from these terms and expressions as, it would result into affecting
the interpretation of law. However, now a days we are simplifying the language where
the strict compliance of the earlier use of the technical words is not warranted so that
Hindi text may be more comprehensible to the extent, a common man would be in a
position to understand the spirit of law. Since law-making process is a continuous one,
no drastic changes can be made. Change can only be gradual. However, Official

27
Languages wing is committed to the task of using easiest Hindi terms and expressions,
which are popular and easily understandable among the people.”
Information regarding simplification of legislative language, as far as it related to the
Regional Language Unit, is given below:
“The translation of Central Acts into eleven regional languages as enshrined in the 8th
Schedule to the Constitution of India is done by respective State Governments through
the Agency/Departments under their control. However, at the time of finalizing the
terminology used in the regional version of different Central Acts, efforts are made to
finalise the terminology, as far as practicable, which is understandable by common man
in that particular region. Officers/officials representing the respective State
Governments in the meeting of Working Group (RL) are also advised during the course
of discussion to adopt simple language so that the purpose of rendering Central Acts
into regional languages is fulfilled.”
7.57 The Committee appreciates that the Ministry has taken steps in the direction of
simplification of laws. But still the Committee feels that it is an ongoing process and efforts
should be made periodically for simplifying the legal language, which is quite often
technical, intricate and incomprehensible for the common man for whom laws are made. It
feels that, laws should be drafted in national or regional languages to convey the purpose
and intent thereof and all Central laws should be translated in order to make the provisions
known to the masses. The Committee, therefore, reiterates that the Ministry should explore
ways and means to simplify laws so as to be understood even by the people having no
specialized knowledge of legal formulations. In other words, Legislative Department should
act as a catalyst for launching a movement for plain language drafting of laws and
instruments of subordinate legislation.
DEPARTMENT OF JUSTICE
8. The Department of Justice forms part of the Ministry of Law and Justice. However,
administrative support to the Department of Justice is provided by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Home Secretary is concurrently Secretary (Justice).
8.1 As per the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961, as amended, from
time to time, the subjects handled by the Department of Justice, inter alia , include the following:—
(i) Appointment, resignation and removal of the Chief Justice of India and Judges of the
Supreme Court of India; their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence (including
leave allowance), pensions and travelling allowance.
(ii) Appointment, resignation and removal, etc. of the Chief Justice and Judges of High
Courts in States, their salaries, rights in respect of leave of absence (including leave
allowances), pensions and travelling allowances.
(iii) Adm inistration of Justice and construction and organisation of courts in the Union
Territories.
(iv) Creation of All India Judicial Service.
(v) Conditions of service of District Judges and other Members of Higher Judicial service
of Union Territories.
(vi) Extension of the Jurisdiction of a High Court to a Union Territory or exclusion of a
Union Territory from the jurisdiction of a High Court.
